title: What I’m hearing about Chargers-Broncos trade bitterness, why Jonathan Taylor stayed Plus, the NFL has an onside kick problem. Jonathan Jones 74

It was all smiles at the Denver Broncos facility Wednesday. One day prior, the reigning AFC West champions had dealt a 2027 fourth-round pick and 2028 fifth-rounder to the Los Angeles Chargers for linebacker Daiyan Henley.

full_text:
Jim Harbaugh and the Chargers were furious about the Broncos trying to renegotiate the Daiyan Henley trade. Luke Hales / Getty Images
It was all smiles at the Denver Broncos facility Wednesday. One day prior, the reigning AFC West champions had dealt a 2027 fourth-round pick and 2028 fifth-rounder to the Los Angeles Chargers for linebacker Daiyan Henley.
Henley spent nearly an hour with general manager George Paton. He toured the facilities. He created social media content for the team. The Broncos even gave him a tablet with the defensive playbook to get him started on things during their bye week.
And then he had to return the tablet. There was a hangup in the trade; in just a few hours, Henley would be returning to L.A.
I talked with sources on all sides of this and across the league, and what I gathered is that each team is certain they went about things the right way.
In the latest What I’m Hearing column, I’ll have nuggets on:
• The timing on Lamar Jackson’s thumb surgery; • Trend watch for the upcoming coaching cycle; • Why the Colts did what they did (and didn’t do); • What Thursday night showed us about the Commanders; • Jerry Jones’ 18-games claim, and why it’s hard to envision; • The NFL’s onside kick problem; • Cam Newton on Bryce Young; • Titans off the air.
But first, the trade that wasn’t.
( Editor’s note: For this column, team and league sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a player on another team or a matter on which they are not authorized to speak publicly.)
League sources say Henley, a fourth-year linebacker, has a known knee issue but it hasn’t prevented him from playing and hasn’t required surgery. He has played in all but one game since 2024, and he has played in 87 percent of the Chargers’ defensive snaps this season.
The winless Chargers had no desire to deal players, much to the chagrin of contending teams hoping to pick over their roster. The deadline neared, and teams called on Henley. The Chargers had a fourth-round offer on the table for the linebacker, who is scheduled to be a free agent in March, but they wanted more for one of their best players.
After considerable back-and-forth, the Broncos added a 2028 fifth-round pick to get it over the finish line. The Chargers dealt their young, well-liked team captain to Denver with a hope that they could actually re-sign him come March. Being able to get two mid-round picks for Henley only to lose him for half of a lost season would be a coup for the team.
The Broncos were aware they might not be able to re-sign Henley in the offseason. Part of Denver’s calculus was that, at worst, he would play so well and be so unaffordable that Denver would get a 2028 compensatory pick after he later signed a big deal elsewhere.
But according to sources in Denver, the medical information the Broncos received did not match what they were learning in real-time after consulting with their own medical team and an independent doctor. The deadline had passed; Paton had a decision to make.
Paton could have proceeded with the agreed-upon deal. He could have outright failed Henley on the physical and sent him back to L.A. He chose option three, which was to attempt to rework the trade terms with the Chargers.
Paton pitched numerous options to the Chargers, per sources, and that is within league rules — Denver consulted with the NFL Management Council. The league would have allowed the pick compensation to change, but a league source says the NFL prohibited adding another player or trading a different player.
Those options Paton pitched included a straight fourth, which the Chargers declined. A fourth and a pick swap was also declined. A fourth and a seventh was turned down. There is a dispute among sources about which side offered this, but I can report that there was a discussion from one side about a fourth plus a conditional fifth that would trigger if Denver signed Henley to an extension at or around the start of the 2027 league year.
The Chargers, multiple sources say, were not interested in renegotiating the deal, believing they had been truthful in their exchanges. L.A. felt as though the passed deadline was being used as leverage; the Bolts would have little recourse but to agree to lesser terms or awkwardly accept the player back. The Broncos felt as though they did what they could to rework a deal with dignity and respect for a player who, according to a league source, they still hope to sign in free agency.
General managers and top executives I spoke with this week had varying opinions on what happened.
“You either walk away or do the deal,” says one GM. “You can’t leverage a deadline for a better deal.”
Says a top executive with another team: “This type of thing happens more often than people realize. The original club either doesn’t know the extent of an injury or downplays it. When the new club does their examination they determine there’s additional risk. They either don’t take the deal or renegotiate the deal. Not a great situation to be in on either side but it happens. The deadline is what makes it look more nefarious.”
Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh made that point on Thursday, saying the league should look into closing a “loophole. … They told us they weren’t going to pass him if it was a fourth and a fifth, which was agreed upon, and they would not pass him for that. They would pass him for a fourth and a … fill in the blank. I don’t know what to call that.”
Harbaugh’s other point was that a physical should be pass/fail. In Henley’s case, Denver would have passed him physically for less compensation. The Broncos believe, and the league rules stipulate, that they are well within their rights to do that.
Considering the number of trades that did not happen in 2026, I expect there to be offseason conversations with the league and competition committee about changes to the rules. The Baltimore Ravens backed out of the Maxx Crosby deal in March when they had issues with the long-term outlook on his knee after going through his physical. A key difference: There was no deadline pressure. Sources said at the time that Ravens GM Eric DeCosta did not attempt to renegotiate the deal.
On Tuesday, the Philadelphia Eagles agreed to trade Arnold Ebiketie to the Cincinnati Bengals for a 2027 sixth-round pick pending a physical. But an hour later Cincinnati broke its agreement when it learned it would also very likely cost the team a 2027 third-round compensatory pick.
That same day the New York Jets sent safety Andre Cisco to the Detroit Lions for a 2028 sixth-round pick that later was adjusted to a 2029 sixth-round pick. Sources tell me that change, over something described as minor, was requested by the Lions and agreed to by the Jets.
In the end, the Chargers will work to mend any potential hard feelings with their homegrown player. The Broncos go forward with their Super Bowl pursuits without a good, young linebacker. And both teams think they will be able to sign Henley five months from now.
Lamar Jackson had surgery on his right thumb last week, I’m told. The Ravens said explicitly in their statement that “recovery timelines are challenging to predict,” but did offer a six-to-10-week timeline.
The full 10 weeks would put Jackson back on the field either in Week 18 against the Bengals or in the wild-card round.
The Ravens are 4-5 and hoping Jacoby Brissett can salvage their season, beginning Monday against the Chargers. The team made clear in a statement attributed to coach Jesse Minter, that it won’t be throwing in the towel on the second half of the season.
“(Jackson) is doing everything he can to get back, and we will let his progress guide the timing of his return,” the statement reads. “We are committed to playing our best football over the second half of the season.”
The Ravens are 2 ½ games behind the Steelers and Bengals for the division lead and 2 ½ games out of a wild-card spot going into this weekend’s games.
We are halfway through the season and every head coach…

title: Vikings-Packers predictions: Can Kirk Cousins revive offense at Lambeau Field? Can the veteran QB make magic in his second stint in purple and gold? Can Brian Flores' defense keep Jordan Love and company in check? Alec Lewis and Jon Krawczynski 22
summary:
The Vikings dealt for veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins ahead of the trade deadline, and they will start him on Sunday in Green Bay. Michael Reaves / Getty Images
Many NFL narratives seem scripted, almost as if too good to be true. This one may have climbed to the top of the list.
Quarterback Kirk Cousins will not only return for the Minnesota Vikings this weekend but also make his first start against the rival Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field, where he last played in purple and gold.
Teammates
full_text:
The Vikings dealt for veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins ahead of the trade deadline, and they will start him on Sunday in Green Bay. Michael Reaves / Getty Images
Many NFL narratives seem scripted, almost as if too good to be true. This one may have climbed to the top of the list.
Quarterback Kirk Cousins will not only return for the Minnesota Vikings this weekend but also make his first start against the rival Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field, where he last played in purple and gold.
Teammates and coach Kevin O’Connell made clear that Cousins does not have to be a hero. But the Vikings offense needs a revival. Perhaps the veteran quarterback can work his magic. What should we expect in this highly anticipated contest? As always, The Athletic ’s Alec Lewis and Jon Krawczynski are here to preview it.
Lewis: Kirk Cousins. Shocker, I know. The storyline is undeniably great. Three years ago, he tore his Achilles tendon at Lambeau Field, and you could feel the weight of the injury. It marked the end. It left his teammates reeling. Now, he returns with an opportunity to turn the tide for the Vikings offense. That’s the 30,000-foot view. The more focused lens falls on what Cousins can provide Sunday. Green Bay likes to play with two deep safeties, so Cousins should be able to check the Vikings in and out of advantageous run looks. In the passing game, Cousins’ processing speed and accuracy should create a more rhythmic feel. I do not expect this reacclimation to go perfectly from the jump. Anything that does not make an efficient forward pass feel like seeing a solar eclipse will work just fine.
Krawczynski: Kirko’s teammates. They needed this. It was crystal clear that the leaps of faith the Vikings were making at quarterback were crashing and burning. The offense wasn’t just struggling. It was the look in the eyes of everyone in the unit. There was hopelessness that was concerning. Whether Cousins has it in his 38-year-old arm to vault the offense into contender status remains unknown. But so many of these Vikings know Cousins. They love and respect him. His presence in the huddle should give a beleaguered group a nice boost. What they do with it remains to be seen, but his familiarity and his spirit are exactly what the Vikings need.
Lewis: Jordan Love, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden. Packers coach Matt LaFleur is doing his best Don Coryell impression right now, allowing his passing game to cook. Love is playing with arm arrogance, and that’s a compliment. Nothing is scaring him from launching the ball to all areas of the field with zero regard for negative outcomes. When the Packers and Vikings matched up in Week 1, Love completed only 50 percent of his passes but accumulated 387 yards. His ability to extend plays by a half-second prevents the Vikings’ pressure from getting in the backfield, and his arm strength makes all areas of the field accessible. Watson and Golden are dynamic. Making Love uncomfortable early will be incumbent on the Vikings’ defense. If he establishes a rhythm with Golden and Watson, it could be a long afternoon.
Krawczynski: Should the Vikings have gone even further at the deadline? Let’s face it, the Cousins trade is an all-in move. They didn’t give up a ton to do it, but it acknowledged that this season is close to going off the rails, and they were willing to swallow their pride and make a move for a 38-year-old quarterback to try to rescue it. So if you’re going that hard, why not trade for Jonathan Taylor as well? Maybe the asking price was too high. But what is too high for a team with a Super Bowl-caliber defense, Super Bowl-caliber special teams and just added a quarterback to try to get the offense up to snuff?
And you could argue that getting Cousins makes it even more important to bolster the running game so you don’t have to put too much on his shoulders. They may have had to empty their coffers to get Taylor, but the NFC is winnable. Maybe now was the right time to pull a Jacksonville Jaguars and get super aggressive. Plus, if it all flamed out, they could recoup some of the assets they gave up by trading Jefferson and rebuilding. And if it all flames out, I don’t think a Jefferson trade is out of the question.
Lewis: Vikings pass rush vs. Packers offensive line. This was not a fair fight in Week 1. Minnesota’s blitzes caused major problems for Green Bay’s interior. The Vikings sacked Love four times. They pressured him 10 times in the fourth quarter. The Packers enter this game with a different group of offensive linemen, and it’ll be interesting to see whether center John Williams and guards Laken Tomlinson and potentially Kevin Zeitler can hold up. It’s also worth monitoring whether the Vikings can activate as many creative blitzes without linebacker Blake Cashman, who is working through the concussion protocol. Playing rookie Jake Golday or Ivan Pace Jr. will affect Minnesota’s defensive strategy.
Krawczynski: Kevin O’Connell vs. Jonathan Gannon. Six weeks ago, the Packers were in free-fall. Their defense allowed 39 points to the Vikings in the opener and 35 to the Atlanta Falcons in Week 3 as they dropped to 1-2. Since then, Gannon has his defense flying around. The unit has given up more than 20 points only once in the last six games, and that was to the New England Patriots in a 45-27 Green Bay blowout last week. O’Connell heard many boos for his offense last week. After acquiring Cousins, the scrutiny on the coach’s play calling will be hotter than ever. And the Packers are playing better defense than anyone the Vikings have faced in recent weeks. It’s gut-check time for O’Connell, who usually gets a very good performance from a QB thrust into duty on short notice.
Lewis: I’m going to throw a curveball. I want to see how many times the Vikings run the football — and how much they can lean on that phase in a game where the quarterback is reacclimating. The Packers have done a solid job of limiting opposing running backs to 4.0 yards per carry (tied for 12th in the league). However, their defensive front leaves a little to be desired. This is why O’Connell could return to the formula that led to early-season success. Cousins’ presence shouldn’t necessitate a bombs-away approach. Even if running backs Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason are only chiseling to 4-yard chunks, the Vikings need to maintain possession and keep the defense off the field. Doing that at Lambeau will make clear what’s possible down the stretch.
Krawczynski: The move to get Cousins was smart. The QB situation was going nowhere fast, and this defense deserves a chance. Cousins returning as a knight in shining armor is an interesting turn of events. But I can’t help but think back to 2010, when the Vikings offense was flailing, and the team acquired an old friend who returned to a hero’s welcome and was assuredly the missing piece. Yet Randy Moss lasted just four games before he left. I do not expect Cousins to berate a catering manager for his return. I also believe that O’Connell has a much better grip on this job than Brad Childress did at the time of the Moss move. The circumstances surrounding the Cousins reunion are much more favorable than when Moss came back. But the stakes feel just as high.
Here is where each team ranks in 2026 in the following categories, using explosive play rate for explosiveness, success rate for efficiency and DVOA’s strength of schedule:
Lewis: Vikings 20, Packers 17. Playing a one-dimensional offense against Flores isn’t optimal. If the Vikings can throw curveballs at Love, they should give their offense enough chances. This is a bet on Cousins’ professionalism. If he cannot raise the offensive floor, larger questions are worth asking.
Krawczynski: Vikings 24, Packers 23. It’s just too juicy to ignore, right? Cousins returning to play in the stadium where his first run as the Vikings’ QB ended? A Minnesota team desperate for a shot in the arm, getting that and more from Kirko Chainz? If Josh Dobbs can…

title: Giants might need to KO a heavyweight or two to make playoffs. That's the way it should be John Harbaugh called his confidence in beating strong opponents "high," even with Jaguars, 49ers, Seahawks and Lions on the schedule. Ian O'Connor 52
summary:

full_text:
Rasul Douglas (29) intercepts a pass intended for Malik Nabers late in the fourth quarter of the Giants' 24-21 loss to the Commanders on Thursday night. Seth Wenig / Associated Press
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The moment J.J. McCarthy threw that pass against the Washington Commanders, New York Giants fans knew they were winning this game and, essentially, the NFC East with it.
How could they not feel that way?
Giants coach John Harbaugh had good cause late Thursday night to call it “probably as good a play as you’re going to see in the National Football League all season.” Washington’s Nick Cross was running right at McCarthy on third down, and though the free blitzer hit the brakes on the MetLife Stadium turf for some ungodly reason, he was still a disconcerting presence in the quarterback’s face.
McCarthy fired as he was getting hit, the ball spiraling into the heart of a Commanders team meeting held at midfield. Isaiah Likely caught it on the Giants’ helmet logo; Sonny Styles and K’Lavon Chaisson crashed into each other; and Likely was off to the races for his 66-yard score that gave the home team a 21-17 lead in the middle of the fourth quarter.
The crowd went wild. Dennard Wilson’s defense was going to take it from there. The Giants were going to be in command of the division at 6-2-1. And Commanders coach Dan Quinn was, perhaps, going to be fired in the aftermath.
But as opportunistic as the Giants have been this year despite season-ending injuries to their franchise player-to-be, Jaxson Dart, and two critical defenders in Brian Burns and Tremaine Edmunds, the Commanders proved to be the rightful victors. They did the little and not-so-little things to complement Jayden Daniels, even outsmarting the rulebook and the refs en route to the win.
With some nifty footwork, Luke McCaffrey turned an in-bounds kickoff into an out-of-bounds kickoff that penalized the Giants and gave the visitors the ball at the 40. (The Commanders did not score on that possession.) With some LeBron James/James Harden-level flopping, Treylon Burks dragged Deonte Banks into a 33-yard pass interference call in the closing minutes. (The Commanders scored the winning points on that possession.)
Meanwhile, the same Giant who had puked on the sideline after eating a pretzel-wrapped hot dog before kickoff froze in his stance as Jameis Winston failed to gain a crucial first down on a quarterback sneak. Harbaugh said Friday that Cam Skattebo, who played a game worthy of the “Iron Man” helmet he wore to the stadium, was not supposed to be shoving Winston from behind because the designed play was not a “tush push.”
But why wasn’t it a “tush push,” given the Giants’ success with that play, and why wasn’t Skattebo or Patrick Ricard or some other raging bull out there driving Winston across the line?
In the end, this was one of many unforced Giants errors in the narrow divide separating winners from losers.
So if the Giants fail to make the playoffs, this 24-21 loss will haunt them until opening day of the 2027 season … and beyond. They could have buried the Commanders like they buried the Eagles four days earlier, but instead the Giants turned the NFC East into a numbers game that might not add up.
The Giants probably need to finish at 8-8-1 or 9-7-1 to win the division, meaning they might need to KO one or two of the relative heavyweights on their schedule. And so be it. The Giants do everything the hard way, so why would this be any different?
They can only play the teams in front of them, as the saying goes, and the win in Houston was impressive, but the truth is they own victories over five teams with a combined record of 13-30. For the Giants to qualify for the playoffs, it would be fitting for them to have to beat at least one legit contender on the way there.
The Giants still have the Jacksonville Jaguars and San Francisco 49ers at home and the Seattle Seahawks and Detroit Lions on the road. Games against the Cleveland Browns at home and the Dallas Cowboys are winnable, but certainly not gimmes. The only seemingly uncontested layups left are the Indianapolis Colts on the road and the Philadelphia Eagles at home.
Though the Giants remain the betting favorites to win the NFC East for the first time since 2011, it appears possible, but unlikely, that they could go 0-4 against the Jaguars, 49ers, Seahawks and Lions and still get that done. They haven’t won at Dallas in a decade, and victories over the Colts, Browns and Eagles alone might not be enough.
Harbaugh called his confidence in beating strong opponents “high” and said his team will take the field expecting to win all eight of its games. “If we win them all, we win them all,” he said, “but we’ll win as many as we can.”
Of course, that mission would feel more attainable at 6-2-1 than 5-3-1.
“We don’t live in that scared world,” Harbaugh said. “Yeah, I said it was an important game before the (Washington) game for that very reason. But now, you don’t sit back and go, ‘Oh no, we’ve got to beat a heavyweight ,’ or whatever you want to call it. It’s the National Football League. We’re planning on going out there and playing and winning the game.
“The so-called heavyweights, I’ve seen them play bad games, too. I’ve seen them have plenty of bad plays. There’s no perfect team in this league. … This is a tough league. It’s pretty even, so we’re in it just like everybody else. … Nobody is going to outfight us — that’s for sure. Nobody is going to outcompete us, without question.”
Harbaugh has indeed brought tenacity to the Giants, who, in recent years, were a wayward cast of Mister Softies in full pads. What right-minded observer would have expected them to stand in first place, two games up in the loss column, after nine games, especially after Dart went down in Week 2?
But even with McCarthy turning his acquisition — in exchange for a fifth-round pick — into the trade of the year, the Giants remain a flawed group. Harbaugh tried in vain to coach around rookie kicker Dominic Zvada, who missed an early 33-yard field-goal attempt, and it cost him on a night that saw too many Giants break down in defining moments.
The Malik Nabers fumble. The Theo Johnson drop. The Jordan Stout shank. The McCarthy “punts” on his final two throws, along with Nabers’ failure to knock down the last one.
Harbaugh and offensive coordinator Matt Nagy were too conservative after a pair of fourth-quarter interceptions handed the Giants golden opportunities to seal the victory against Washington, and that was that.
“It absolutely sucks,” McCarthy said.
So will the experience of watching Sunday’s games after losing Thursday night.
“It’s going to be a long weekend,” Harbaugh said. But the coach promised his team would rebound with a fearless approach and a spirit shaped by “power and courage.”
Yes, the Giants will need all of that to prove they belong with the big boys in the postseason.

full_text:
DeForest Buckner has made a habit of putting in extra work. Now, younger teammates have followed his example. Brooke Sutton / Getty Images
SANTA CLARA, Calif. — There are the calls for the ball from the nearby soccer field, mixed in with the occasional honk of a car horn. Onlookers will look over, possibly wondering … isn’t that large man DeForest Buckner?
It is, as the 49ers’ 6-foot-7 defensive tackle hits a field at a park around the corner from Levi’s Stadium two nights a week for more drills long after the team’s practice is over. Last week, teammate Mykel Williams tagged along. On Wednesday, Osa Odighizuwa also punched in for some extra work.
“Just fine-tuning some stuff with some technique work and drills,” Buckner said. “I do it to stay sharp with my handwork and hand placement and things like that.”
A post shared by Mark Hall (@markhall___enterprises)
Buckner has been working with personal defensive line trainer Mark Hall since 2019, and Hall came out west with Buckner when the 49ers reacquired the 32-year-old two weeks ago in a deal with the Indianapolis Colts. The pair break down film every week (Monday on the previous game, Tuesday on the next opponent) before honing Buckner’s technique on Wednesday and Thursday.
When he returned to town, the 11-year veteran immediately assumed a leadership role with a very young defensive line. Rookie Romello Height started joining Buckner for 5:30 a.m. weightlifting sessions, while Williams asked him what else he does during the week.
“He is a great role model, and with role models, you want to be like them,” Williams said. “So I asked him if I can join him in the park, and he said yeah. It went great. I have been learning a lot.”
The night sessions last about an hour and allow players to focus on something they just don’t have a lot of time for in practice. Players work on striking-hand usage and the angles with which they attack blockers, as well as where to look while working on their technique.
“These young guys are eager to learn,” Buckner said. “And I want them to continue to see how to approach each week like a pro.”
The young players had a welcome gift for Buckner when he arrived, or at least defensive tackle C.J. West did. He voluntarily gave up his No. 99 jersey so the veteran could keep his number. West didn’t ask Buckner for anything in return but said he made out well in the end.
“He took care of me for sure,” West said, smiling.
The 49ers’ veterans are also quite happy that Buckner is back.
“He set the culture for us back in ’19, and he’s doing the same now,” defensive end Nick Bosa said.

I think the biggest thing is watching the film, seeing what we want to do, and then ultimately trying to go out there and execute our plan.”

title: Game-by-Game Arizona Cardinals Predictions for the Rest of the 2026 Season
full_text:
After a brutal stretch of games to start the 2026 season, the Arizona Cardinals' second half of the season features some more winnable matchups.
With eight games left, their opponents' combined record is 32-36-1. With an easier schedule, how can this team wrap up what has been, so far, not a great year?
While the Cardinals upset the Rams in SoFi Stadium, I predict they'll lose here at home. With all the injuries both teams are facing in their receiving corps, this has a high chance of being more of a defensive game.
Since neither offense is going to be at full power, the question remains: which team has the better defense?
That team is Los Angeles. The Rams have one of the best defensive duos with edge rusher Myles Garrett and defensive tackle Aaron Donald. Garrett is coming off of an amazing performance against the Washington Commanders.
In that game, Garrett had three sacks and three tackles for loss. Against a shaky offensive line, the Rams' high-powered defensive line is enough to secure the win against Arizona in rookie quarterback Carson Beck's first start.
Yes, miracles can happen in the NFL, and I am predicting one here as the Cardinals go into Arrowhead to knock off the dynastic Chiefs. While Kansas City does have a lot of high-impact offensive players, such as quarterback Patrick Mahomes , tight end Travis Kelce, and running back Kenneth Walker, they have had some poor offensive outings this season.
In Arizona's wins this year, it's been because their defense has played well. While it's an inconsistent unit, they do have their good games. The Chiefs have struggled dealing with pressure this year, as shown in their losses to the Seattle Seahawks and the Denver Broncos. The Cardinals' defensive line is one of the best parts of their defense. If they keep the pressure on Mahomes, that could bode well for a win.
Now, even if Arizona's defense gets some pressure and sacks on Mahomes, he has shown he can still make big plays in a short amount of time. This is where quarterback Beck's strengths come in. In the preseason, Beck was great at getting the ball out and keeping the offense in a rhythm. This could be just enough for Arizona to edge out a huge win this year.
After beating Kansas City and barely losing to Los Angeles, the Cardinals suffer a big home loss. The main reason is that the last time Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels faced this Arizona defense, he was very efficient in both the air and on the ground.
During Week 4 of the 2024 season, Daniels passed for 233 yards, ran for 47 yards, and threw and rushed for touchdowns to help Washington get a big win.
Additionally, the Commanders have rookie linebacker Sonny Styles. Styles has had a great rookie year for Washington, especially in coverage. In the NFL, linebackers usually cover tight ends, so Styles could take away some potential big plays from Cardinals tight end Trey McBride.
The Cardinals finish playing the NFC East in what could be one of the ugliest games of the entire NFL season. Arizona and Philadelphia have each had horrid losses and ugly moments this year. It comes down to the better offense, which goes to the Cardinals. This is because it seems that whether it's Tanner McKee or Joe Milton at quarterback for the Eagles, they can not move the ball.
While Beck has yet to play in an NFL regular-season game, if he can translate his preseason success to the regular season, it could be enough for a very sloppy game. Also, it seems like in this century, Arizona has had Philadelphia's number whenever the Cardinals host.
After Arizona's bye week, I expect a huge win against the Jets. While the Jets offense has some good rookie playmakers, enough for them to put up a respectable 23 points, New York's defense is a mess.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur could scheme up some great plays, especially in the pass game. The Jets' secondary has been their biggest weakness this season, so Beck could have the best game of his career to help Arizona win.
This is a very weird game, as the Saints have looked very hot and cold this season. One week, it looks like they could win the NFC South; the next, it looks like they could be picking top five in the draft. However, I do think New Orleans gets the edge because their offense is more electric.
With Cardinals wideout Michael Wilson done for the year, the Cardinals' receiving room isn't in the best shape. Meanwhile, the Saints have Chris Olave, a great wideout, and rookie receiver Jordyn Tyson returns to the state where he played college football.
Additionally, New Orleans quarterback Tyler Shough has shown some good growth as a passer in his second year. Now, Arizona could get this win down south, as the Saints' defense has been pretty porous this year. However, in a close game, I think the Cardinals lose their last road game of the season.
Arizona finishes up the AFC West in a game that, while not inspiring much confidence in their defense, could be a fun shootout that goes Las Vegas' way. This will be a battle of the rookie quarterbacks, with Fernando Mendoza leading the Raiders and Beck leading the Cardinals. It is a rematch of the College Football Championship, where Mendoza was victorious.
I believe Las Vegas takes this because Mendoza is a better quarterback than Beck. While I do think Beck is a fine player, the Raiders took Mendoza number one for a reason. With Las Vegas's defense being poor, Beck could have some great moments this game. However, Mendoza's clutchness shows up for the Raiders as they win on a last-second field goal in Glendale.
Well, after an exciting game, Arizona plummets to earth as they get destroyed by San Francisco. For starters, head coach Kyle Shanahan and quarterback Brock Purdy are too much for this Cardinals defense to handle.
There is also a high chance the 49ers are fighting for the NFC West or the NFC's No. 1 seed. Sometimes, during Week 18, teams rest their starters, but that is very unlikely for San Francisco.
Overall, I predict the Cardinals win three out of their final eight games, with some close losses. This will make their end-of-season record 6-11. Beck and the offense could provide some fun moments, but the Cardinals still have much work to do, especially on defense, which should be the team's main focus after the 2026 season is complete.

title: Bold Predictions: Carson Beck Leads Cardinals' Second-Half Charge
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' 3-6 start to the season has been underwhelming yet above expectations all in the same swoop.
3-6 isn't nearly close enough for the postseason or division title, though they've practically matched their projected 2026 win total halfway through the year.
The roster looks drastically different than it did at the beginning of the season. Nobody has been fired, though moves could be coming if losing continues.
Three bold predictions before the second half of the year gets underway:
All eyes are on Carson Beck for this final stretch of games.
The third-round pick is now inserted into starting duties under center for Arizona, and fair or not, the Cardinals will use these games to make a serious decision on their future at quarterback.
By all accounts, Beck is ready for the moment. He believes so and the Cardinals believe so, too. Though he's battling a patchwork offensive line and lack of weapons outside of Trey McBride, head coach and play-caller Mike LaFleur should be able to open up the playbook and let Beck rip it.
Make no mistake: This is a massive hill for Beck to climb. However, he's been able to sit for the first half of the season and log mental reps before being thrown into the fire. That, combined with his college experience and traits, could make for some fun games down the back end of the schedule.
We initially projected Rallis to be fired before the bye week, but that doesn't look like it's happening. While Arizona's defense is still below par, the Cardinals have turned things around on his side of the ball — just enough to buy him more time.
At this point, with Rallis' contract reportedly up at the end of this season, it feels like Arizona will keep Rallis in his seat barring a dramatic nosedive.
As for Ossenfort, it feels unlikely owner Michael Bidwill will fire his general manager in-season. The Cardinals' GM is under contract through the 2027 season, and while he could very well be dismissed before a big offseason, the trade deadline's passing doesn't leave much reason for Bidwill to make a move during the season.
Two hot-seat names entering the year will stick around through the end of the schedule, even with a mere three wins thus far.
Do you know how good you have to be to unseat Garrett Williams?
King's had a strong season as Arizona's slot cornerback, ranking as one of Pro Football Focus' highest-graded defensive backs this season. Williams has played just nine snaps in the last two weeks as a result of King's emergence.
Alongside King, previous afterthoughts in Max Melton and Denzel Burke have played extremely well this season.

title: Midseason Report Card: Grading Cardinals Coaches Through First Half of 2026
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are halfway through the 2026 season, and quite frankly, have surpassed expectations already.
With a 3-6 record, that doesn't exactly roll off the tongue right — though the Cardinals have already reached their projected win total. Signs of a promising future haven't exactly been bountiful, though they've been spotted nonetheless.
Before the second half of the regular season gets underway, let's grade the Cardinals' three top coaches:
This was perhaps the toughest evaluation.
On one hand, the Cardinals' defense has picked up their play in recent weeks. Rallis has recently found his old (and arguably more successful) calling card in aggressive play-calling and creative sim-pressures. That's led to a fairly drastic step up in production as of late, a positive sign for a coordinator who was very much on the hot seat early this season.
However, when taking a step back and evaluating the entire year's performance thus far, it's incredibly hard to forget just how bad Arizona's defense was. Despite the drastic increase in play, the Cardinals have still allowed 30+ points in all but three games this season.
Numbers aren't everything, though Arizona still ranks near the bottom of the league in several different categories — both standard and advanced analytics.
Right now, it's tough to say Rallis is in jeopardy of losing his job. However, that could easily change with a bad performance or two.
Not quite passing, not quite failing. Rallis' recent performances still give hope for a turnaround, but this feels like a very favorable grade.
Special teams is a bit tougher to evaluate, though the third (and often forgotten about) phase of the game can easily help win or lose games.
New coordinator Michael Ghobrial has the Cardinals in the top third in the league in kickoff return yardage allowed (25.4). On his own return unit, they're tied for the most amount of kickoff returns for 20+ yards at 39.
Kickoffs have been fairly contained defensively while the Cardinals have made some nice returns on their own accord.
Punting, meanwhile, is dead last at 43.9 yards per punt. For a team that is tied for the third-most amount of punts, we've got plenty of sample size. As for their punt returns, their 7.9 yards per return is eighth-worst in the NFL.
Not exactly a glowing endorsement.
Field goals have been fairly strong for Arizona, as their only missed attempts have been from 50+ yards this season. They rank near the top of the league with their 90%+ conversion rate while they haven't had a field goal blocked – though Chad Ryland did miss an extra point in Dallas.
Ghobrial's done a fairly good job in his first season.
This is an overall mixed evaluation between the offense and his management of the team as a first-year head coach.
It's hard to truly say how much of Arizona's 3-6 start rests on LaFleur's shoulders, as ultimately he shoulders the blame or carries the praise based off the team's overall results while numerous factors such as schedule, poor roster construction and injuries also are legitimate. The truth likely resides somewhere in the middle of those two schools of thought.
Offensively, the Cardinals have been less than desirable — to say the least. Subpar quarterback play and injuries practically everywhere have really weighed the unit down, though some of LaFleur's play-calling and situational decision-making has also been questionable.
However, we've seen glimpses of how strong the offense can be when all cylinders are firing, giving us a taste of the potential that made LaFleur a desirable coaching hire earlier this year. Regardless, the Cardinals' offense has been mostly underwhelming, and that falls first on LaFleur's headset.
His overall handling of what's been a brutal first season as a head coach has been impressive, however. It doesn't feel as if the Cardinals' locker room has given up while he's remained just as energetic and process-driven as the first week of the season.
That's not easy. Losing wears on you. But LaFleur is patient and knows that patience is needed if the Cardinals are going to get where they want.
LaFleur's grade feels like a tug-of-war between the reality of Arizona's 3-6 record and approaching the situation with nuance. LaFleur is by no means a bust or bad head coach. I'm still incredibly high on him and his future.
While that should improve over the coming months, we're grading his performance here and now — which isn't quite failing, though there's much room for improvement.

title: How Safe Is Mike LaFleur's Job With Cardinals After Rocky Start?
full_text:
Arizona Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur has already led the team for nine weeks in his first season. During that time, Arizona has endured some very ugly moments and losses. While that stems from poor teambuilding and management, it also falls on the head coach.
What areas has LaFleur been at fault for, and could the Cardinals move on from him?
During his tenure, LaFleur's offense in Arizona has lacked much of the creativity and excitement usually associated with a play-calling trees under Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay. Across the league, many play callers from that tree (Liam Coen of the Jacksonville Jaguars, Klint Kubiak of the Las Vegas Raiders, and Mike's brother, Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers ) have shown the great play-calling many Cardinal fans expected from LaFleur.
The poor play-calling has really reared its ugly head in the red zone. After Week 9, Arizona ranks last in red-zone TD percentage at just 44%. While the Cardinals' offense has major personnel issues, many of its top players including tight end Trey McBride has the tools and traits to be great red-zone targets.
Before calling plays for the Cardinals, LaFleur did the same for the New York Jets. LaFleur lasted only two years with the Jets, from 2021-22. The biggest issue with LaFleur in New York was his inability to develop quarterback Zach Wilson, who was drafted in 2021 and showed great traits coming out of BYU.
Of all LaFleur's issues, this is the most worrying. If Arizona fans want a great quarterback in next year's class, LaFleur's poor development of Wilson could be considered a huge red flag.
While this might seem like a crazy idea to let a head coach go after one season, it has happened in the NFL, specifically with this team. Eight years ago, the Cardinals fired Steve Wilks after just one season.
Before joining Arizona, Wilks was the defensive coordinator for the Carolina Panthers. The Panthers' defense during this era was one of the league's better units. The Wilks hire was seen as a solid move, yet after one bad year, he was gone.
Speaking of Cardinals coaches, their offensive coordinator, Nathaniel Hackett , is another example. Hackett was hired in 2022 to be the head coach of the Denver Broncos. However, he did not complete his first year, as he was fired before the season even ended.
During this decade, eight head coaches have been fired after just one season. That list includes big names like Pete Carroll after his 2025 stint with the Las Vegas Raiders and Urban Meyer after coaching the Jacksonville Jaguars in 2021. If Arizona does let LaFleur go after one season, it wouldn't be eye-opening by NFL standards.
However, the biggest reason the Cardinals could move on from LaFleur is how many amazing head-coaching candidates there are. From offensive-minded coordinators to defensive gurus to proven coaches, this upcoming cycle has them all.
Starting with the latter, Mike Tomlin could be an option. Many Arizona fans have bad taste with Tomlin's Pittsburgh Steelers, as they beat the Cardinals in Super Bowl 43. However, Tomlin never had a losing record with the Steelers and made the postseason 13 times during his 19-year tenure with Pittsburgh.
Sean McDermott, who recently coached the Buffalo Bills, could also be a tremendous option. McDermott, who coached the Bills for eight years, helped build a winning culture and develop quarterback Josh Allen.
Among defensive coordinators who could be head coaches, what better option is there than Brian Flores? Flores has done an amazing job with the Minnesota Vikings defense this year. There is also Anthony Campanile, whom the Cardinals did interview last year before hiring LaFleur.
On the offensive side, there are some exciting and intriguing names, including Baltimore Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, Jaguars offensive coordinator Grant Udinski, and Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy. Each has a different approach to building explosive, fun offenses.
Overall, LaFleur could be an amazing head coach. There are glimpses of great moments. However, the lack of consistency and a strong head-coaching pool just might push Arizona to move on.
Ultimately, time will tell how the Cardinals' head coaching job turns out.

title: 3 Biggest Things Carson Beck Said Before First Cardinals Start
full_text:
ARIZONA – The Carson Beck era is officially set to begin this weekend.
After the Arizona Cardinals announced Beck would be their starter in Week 10 , all eyes now gear towards the rookie third-round pick to finish out the season as the team's starting quarterback. How he performs in this final stretch will likely determine if he's sitting in the seat come 2027.
Beck met with reporters ahead of his first start — here's the three biggest things he said:
Beck when asked if he can carry confidence into his first ever start:
“Of course. I think the coolest thing about confidence is that confidence is a choice. With that also, I’ve said it before, it makes everyone else around you better as well. It exudes confidence into them when you’re showing that you’re confident.
"When you can choose that, again, you just have to go out there and execute. You have to go out there and do your thing and you have to go out there and be confident, have swag, and have moxie. Regardless of the circumstances, regardless of anything going on around you, regardless of maybe what happened the play before or maybe thinking about what’s going to happen the next play.
"You have to be in the present moment and that’s really all you can do and control.”
Beck on handling the spotlight of being a starting quarterback:
"I feel like I've done it for a long time. The past three years — having started at some of the biggest college programs in the country, having been a top five team (and) a number one team in the country —  you have the national spotlight. Obviously, it's a lot different now being in the NFL — (it) being such a huge product and what it is.
"Honestly, just be myself. Be there for my teammates, be selfless (and) do what I can for everyone around me. Then ultimately go out there and give my best effort, have confidence and just be relentless. I think that's how you handle that and there is really no more to it."
When asked if Mike LaFleur has given him any advice:
"There's this quote that (Head) Coach (Mike) LaFleur said — I don't remember if it was before a game or during training camp but he showed a clip of (Golden State Warriors Guard Stephen) 'Steph' Curry and he was essentially talking about the shot that he had in the USA versus France game. It's like, 'Being comfortable with not knowing what the outcome is going to be and then going out there and shooting your shot.' I think that's how you handle the emotions of it because obviously all of us care a ton.
"I care a ton, right? You want to go out there, you want to do good (and) you want to play your best but when you think too much about that and you fear failure or you fear not having the result that you want, that's when the emotions get in the way. I think just being comfortable with not knowing the outcome and then ultimately going and shooting your shot is how you handle those emotions."

title: Official Cardinals-Rams Week 10 Injury Report Revealed
full_text:
The first official injury report for Week 10's clash at State Farm Stadium between the Los Angeles Rams and Arizona Cardinals has been revealed.
Nearly 25 names — some larger than others — appear after Wednesday's practice. The report will change after the team's practice on Thursday and Friday, though for now, here's what both sides look like in terms of health:
DNP - Budda Baker (rest), Hjalte Froholdt (concussion), Jon Gaines II (ankle), Roy Lopez (toe/ankle), Isaac Seumalo (rest), Josh Sweat (rest), Mack Wilson Sr. (rest/knee/ankle)
LIMITED - Zach Carter (knee), Bam Knight (concussion), Hunter Long (knee), Max Melton (knee/hand), Dante Stills (shoulder), Jayden Williams (knee), Andrew Wingard (groin)
The big story of the day out of Arizona was Carson Beck officially being named the team's starting quarterback for this weekend, propping the third-round pick up for this first taste of action all season.
“Absolutely. Yes. Any of these guys. Real excited for Carson. Excited for the guys that are going to be catching the ball for him, particularly in the receiver room," Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said today. Arizona's WR room has also been decimated due to injury.
"I think our receiver coach (said) there’s five total catches amongst that whole group this year. Obviously, (WR) Zay (Jones) has caught some balls and stuff like that if he ends up being the one up, but (I’m) excited for all these guys to have a great opportunity to go compete this Sunday.”

Puka Nacua is the biggest story in Los Angeles, as the star wideout previously was expected to land on injured reserve — though now that's not the case. However, he's expected to miss Week 10 against Arizona.
With star wideout Davante Adams also out, the Rams could very much be depleted in their road trip to State Farm Stadium this week.
Los Angeles is hoping for a dash of revenge following their earlier upset to the Cardinals at SoFi Stadium — we'll see if Sean McVay is able to learn more from a loss than a win.

title: NFL Insider Rips Cardinals' Surprising Budda Baker Decision
full_text:
ARIZONA — Arizona Cardinals safety Budda Baker was perhaps the biggest name that wasn't moved ahead of the league's 2026 trade deadline, ensuring the franchise legend remains with the team through 2026.
It wasn't for lack of suitors.
Baker had numerous teams that did extensive work on him at the deadline according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz.
"The trade that I thought had the best chance of happening in terms of a big name that didn't was Budda Baker to Buffalo. Now Jacksonville also made the big deal for Jessie Bates, the All-Pro from Atlanta, they also took a long look at Budda Baker. But Arizona, ultimately, was not willing to pull the trigger and it was a little hard for me to understand," said Schultz.
"They're going nowhere. The Cardinals are going nowhere this season. You have a Day 2 pick and probably more you could have gotten out of Buffalo. ... Budda Baker's given them everything. He's been there a decade. He's been to eight Pro Bowls, he's been an All-Pro. That's the type of thing where I just thought the organization should have done right by him."
The #Cardinals decided not to trade Budda Baker to the #Bills , and I struggle to understand why not. Great chopping it up with my guy @CSimmsQB today. https://t.co/2nOnucQvVS pic.twitter.com/nLf6SWOlon
The Bills' offer for Baker was reportedly around a second-round pick, which Arizona declined. Along with Jacksonville, the Detroit Lions were another team believed to be interested in Baker.
The 3-6 Cardinals ultimately didn't trade anybody at the deadline after previously dealing Jacoby Brissett and Marvin Harrison Jr. — Baker, Josh Sweat and even Garrett Williams were possible trade candidates.
Baker's one of the few players who (at least should) have the right to determine his future after spending the last ten seasons in the desert, emerging as a top player in the league and a pillar of a Cardinals franchise that hasn't seen much success since he arrived.
His name has always been involved in trade chatter, though 2026 felt like the most realistic possibility of a trade after Baker reportedly was open to a move to a contender, though he never officially put a trade request in and was open to whatever the future had in store.
Despite Buffalo being an ideal landing spot for Baker in terms of a win-now team along with the aggressive draft capital to make a deal happen, the Cardinals kept the face of the franchise around.
After 2026, Baker has one year remaining on his deal in Arizona. He will turn 31 in January.

title: Cardinals Finally Deliver Carson Beck News Fans Have Been Waiting For
full_text:
TEMPE — The Arizona Cardinals finally delivered the news fans have been waiting for.
Head coach Mike LaFleur confirmed on Wednesday that rookie third-round pick Carson Beck would start ahead of the team's Week 10 matchup against the Los Angeles Rams.
Beck gets the nod after the Cardinals lost previous starter Gardner Minshew to a season-ending UCL injury on Sunday.
"Go out and operate. Go operate this offense and go play," LaFleur said on what he wants to see out of Beck on Sunday. "Each play is his own. So do what he's been doing in practice. It's just an extension of the practice field. Obviously, it's live bullets, and go operate, go play his game."
The Cardinals are 3-6 on the season, and after the trade deadline has come and gone, they're officially turning the page towards the future with Beck — who will have the second half of Arizona's season as an evaluation for the front office ahead of a 2027 offseason where the Cardinals very well could pursue a quarterback.
Beck's extensive college experience at Georgia and Miami on top of successfully leading both programs to a national championship appearance made him an attractive late day two pick.
The plan wasn't initially for Beck to play this early in the season — especially against a loaded Rams defense with Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett — though LaFleur believes his passer is ready.
"You never really know until you get to the live bullets on Sunday," LaFleur continued on Beck.
"But just the way he goes about his business, whether it's been from OTAs through training camp before he got hurt, obviously seeing him operate there in that first half [preseason] plus the one you know possession there in the second half. So obviously we'll know more come that Sunday, but have all the confidence that he's ready to roll."

title: Jessie Bates III Recalls ‘Teary-Eyed’ Falcons Goodbye after Trade to Jaguars
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons may not have enjoyed the on-field success that Jessie Bates III may have hoped for.
But the franchise is dear in the star free safety’s heart after spending 3.5 seasons in Flowery Branch.
The All-Pro selections and his momentum-swinging defensive plays, including his ball-hawking interceptions and patented rendition of the “Peanut Punch,” come secondary to the impact he and the franchise had on each other as he heads to the Jacksonville Jaguars via trade .
“You spend somewhere four years; you create relationships, you create bonds that’ll last a lifetime,” Bates told Juston Lewis of the Jacksonville-Times Union .
“There are people over there from the staff, the players, the janitors, the cafeteria people – those are my people. I would see those people every single day, and they did a lot for me. So there’s so much appreciation and love for those guys and girls over there.”
Bates was the first move Atlanta made as sellers in this year’s trade deadline .
On Monday, the Falcons moved the nine-year NFL veteran to Jacksonville for a 2027 NFL Draft second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder.
It marked the end of an era for one of Atlanta’s fan favorites who withstood three different coaches, no playoff appearances, and a world of “what-ifs.”
Bates had become a staple for the Falcons, having been named a team captain and sharing a locker with potential franchise quarterback Michael Penix Jr.
Now he leaves behind the foundation he’s built for a fresh start for a Super Bowl contender.
“It was tough,” Bates said when asked about the moment he departed the Falcons facility. “When I left that building, there were teary eyes from myself and coaches, trainers, equipment guys – a lot of love there. I take pride in not just being a great football player, but just being a great person, being a great light in the building.”
The rationale behind the Bates-to-Jags trade was that the Falcons looked as though they weren’t going to re-sign the safety as he entered unrestricted free agency following the season. At 29, Bates’ age was a factor in the decision, as the Falcons look to start a youth movement and build through the draft .
The Bates move predated the Falcons getting another draft pick for starting center Ryan Neuzil . He was traded on Tuesday to the Baltimore Ravens for guard Andrew Vorhees on an expiring deal and a conditional 2028 sixth-round pick.
On Friday, the Falcons inked younger players to multiyear deals, defensive end Cameron Thomas (three years, $33 million) and cornerback CJ Henderson (two years, $20 million) .
Fans will have to wait to see Bates' debut for the Jaguars. Head coach Liam Coen said Bates will not play against the 1-7 Titans, with no bye week a factor. The Jaguars have already had their bye, but the Falcons haven't. His decision gives Bates the week off that he didn't get with the Falcons.
Meanwhile, the Falcons (3-6) will make their first post-Bates appearance when the Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) come to town for an NFL Week 10 clash. DeMarcco Hellams is expected to step into the free safety role. The Falcons enter their bye week after facing the Chiefs.
Kickoff is also at 1 p.m. and will be aired on CBS.

title: Falcons' Biggest Defensive Problem Is Becoming Impossible to Ignore
full_text:
ATLANTA – The Atlanta Falcons are coming off the fourth loss in five games, and they just traded away their best defender , Jessie Bates III. A once-dominant run defense is reeling, having allowed 98 yards or more in each of those games.
Not to say the Falcons have always struggled against the run, because they haven’t.
In the first four weeks, they allowed 193 combined yards (2.7 yards per carry) and were the NFL’s best run defense by a wide margin. Then, Derrick Henry and the Ravens ran wild in Week 5, piling up 208 yards on the ground. From there, it snowballed, and the Falcons have been the league’s third-worst team since that overtime loss.
And the defensive issues haven’t stopped there.
The Falcons were eighth in defensive EPA, second in defensive success rate, and leading the league in quarterback pressure rates over those first four weeks. But like the run defense, those numbers have plummeted to 22nd, 30th, and 21st in the games since.
Injuries to Za’Darius Smith, Samson Ebukam, and Divine Deablo in the front seven have hurt, as have the absences of C.J. Henderson and A.J. Terrell Jr. on the back end. But Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich was the first to take ownership of the sharp regression, saying the team has been playing well below expectations.
“That's the 100% truth, and I think everybody is taking that upon themselves,” Ulbrich said Wednesday. “I do feel fortunate that we have a group of a bunch of thumb pointers, where [it’s], ‘What can I do more?’ I feel like we have that collectively.”
But these issues start on the ground, the proclaimed identity of this Falcons’ defense.
“We're just not playing it well enough, so that's me, from a scheme perspective, making sure that we're getting guys in the right spaces to be successful,” he said. “At times, we've done that and didn't play well enough. There are times we didn't do that (scheme-wise), and it wasn’t on the players; it was 100% on coaching.
“We all have to do more and do better in regard to defending the run.”
The numbers have been scary, but the defensive coordinator insisted there is no ‘panic’ within the locker room about getting back on track, but there might be if these issues continue on into Sunday. The Kansas City Chiefs are coming to town, and there is no room for error in a game like this.
A unit typically known for its future Hall of Fame quarterback Patrick Mahomes is now feared for what it can do on the ground. Kenneth Walker III (872) ranks second only to Bijan Robinson (880) in rushing yards and threatens to continue the Falcons' run-defense slide.
Ulbrich said stopping a back like this is going to “take all 11.” Walker can get downhill quickly and create havoc at the second level if defenders don’t stick to their run fits or tackle well.
“That's where we have to be at our best. And it's a unique challenge in that way because there's not a whole lot of backs like him,” he explained. “On top of all that, he has gas. He has real finishing speed, and he's a guy that can hit the home run at any time. There's a reason I think he's the first- or second-most efficient runner in the league right now. It’s going to be a great challenge.”
Walker will be the next big challenge for the Falcons, but stopping a back like this is what they want to be known for. Doing it consistently has eluded them in recent weeks.
“I've never been a part of a great defense that didn't defend the run well,” Ulbrich said. “That has to become part of who we are. That has to become part of our identity. And right now it is not.”
The 3-6 Falcons still have time to rediscover the defensive identity that made them one of the NFL's best units early in the season. Those opportunities are running out.
With the bye week coming after Sunday's matchup, the Falcons desperately need to respond against Walker and the Chiefs. If they can't, their season could slip further out of reach, and they have one glaring issue to blame.

title: Falcons Sign Redeemed CB to 2-Year Contract Extension
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are rewarding one of their biggest defensive surprises this season, agreeing to a two-year contract extension with cornerback C.J. Henderson. The deal is worth up to $20 million with $11 million guaranteed, according to Ian Rapoport , tying the team financially to Henderson for next season with a club option in 2028.
Henderson was the second of two extensions announced by the Falcons on Friday. Edge rusher Cameron Thomas got a three-year deal worth up to $33 million as well.
Henderson stepped into a starting outside cornerback role after A.J. Terrell suffered an injury in Week 2 and has taken full advantage of the opportunity.
What initially appeared to be a temporary replacement assignment has turned into a breakout season for the veteran defensive back, who has established himself as an important piece of Atlanta’s secondary. He was officially moved ahead of Mike Hughes on the depth chart this week.
The two-year extension gives Henderson additional security while allowing the Falcons to retain a player who has become increasingly valuable to their defense. PFF has him as the No. 22-ranked cornerback in the NFL, the highest of any Falcons player.
Through eight games, Henderson has recorded 41 total tackles, 32 solo tackles, nine passes defended, and one forced fumble. His nine pass breakups are already a career high, surpassing his previous best of six, which he recorded during the 2020 and 2022 seasons.
His production has been particularly impressive considering the circumstances surrounding his expanded role. Henderson entered the season competing for opportunities in Atlanta’s secondary, but Terrell’s injury created an opening that he has not relinquished.
The 28-year-old has demonstrated the ability to handle consistent responsibilities on the outside while providing the Falcons with another dependable option in coverage. His performance has also helped Atlanta navigate an important injury in its defensive backfield without having to completely overhaul its secondary.
Henderson’s emergence is especially notable given his NFL journey. The Jacksonville Jaguars selected him ninth overall in the 2020 NFL Draft out of Florida. He spent the first part of his career in Jacksonville before moving to the Carolina Panthers, where he played three seasons.
After appearing in just four games with Atlanta last season, Henderson has found a much larger opportunity in 2026. He entered the year with 33 career starts and has continued to build on that experience with an expanded role.
For general manager Ian Cunningham and the Falcons, extending Henderson represents an investment in a player who has earned a larger place in the team’s defensive plans.
Henderson has earned a starting spot at one of the outside corners, which could push Avieon Terrell inside to nickel. Billy Bowman Jr. hasn't been able to stay healthy long enough to solidify a spot there, and Sydney Brown is a depth piece forced to play starting minutes.
The extension also provides some continuity for a secondary that has dealt with personnel changes throughout the season.
Henderson arrived in Atlanta looking for an opportunity to reestablish himself in the NFL. He delivered the best statistical season of his career and earned a two-year extension from the Falcons.

title: Falcons Edge Cameron Thomas Gets Significant Contract Extension
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are rewarding one of their biggest defensive surprises, agreeing to a three-year contract extension with edge rusher Cameron Thomas worth up to $33 million, according to the team.
The agreement keeps Thomas under contract with the Falcons through the 2029 season. Equity Sports CEO Chris Cabott, Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham, and senior vice president Bryce Johnston finalized the deal Thursday night.
For Thomas, the extension represents a significant career turnaround after spending several seasons searching for consistency and an opportunity to establish himself in the NFL.
A third-round pick by the Arizona Cardinals in 2022, Thomas initially struggled to find his footing in the league. He recorded three sacks as a rookie but managed just 19 tackles and no sacks in 15 appearances during his second season.
His career took another turn in 2024 when Arizona traded him to the Kansas City Chiefs. However, his opportunity in Kansas City never developed, as he appeared in just four games before eventually joining the Cleveland Browns.
Cleveland provided Thomas with an opportunity to rebuild his career. He appeared in five games with the Browns in 2024, recording 10 tackles and one sack.
Thomas returned to Cleveland for the 2025 season and played in all 17 games. He finished with 27 tackles and 2.5 sacks, establishing career highs in several defensive categories and demonstrating his ability to contribute as part of an NFL defensive rotation.
That production caught Atlanta’s attention.
The Falcons signed Thomas to a one-year contract in March 2026 , giving him another opportunity to prove he could become a consistent contributor. The move has turned into a significant success for Cunningham and Atlanta’s front office.
Through nine games in the 2026 season, Thomas has recorded 25 tackles, two sacks, one forced fumble and one pass deflection. He has also generated 25 quarterback pressures, according to Pro Football Focus.
His emergence has been particularly important for a Falcons defense looking to maintain consistent pressure on opposing quarterbacks. Thomas has provided another productive option along the defensive front while demonstrating the versatility to contribute against the run and pass.
Now, Atlanta is making sure he remains part of its plans.
The three-year extension worth up to $33 million is a substantial reward for a player who joined the organization on a one-year deal just months ago.
Thomas has gone from struggling to find a consistent role in Kansas City to becoming a starting-caliber contributor in Atlanta. The Falcons clearly believe his best football is still ahead of him, and the new agreement gives him an opportunity to continue building on his breakout through the 2029 season.

title: Falcons Trade Deadline Moves Tell One Story, Atlanta’s Leaders Tell Another
full_text:
After dropping to 3-6 and becoming trade-deadline sellers, the resounding narrative has been that the Atlanta Falcons are mailing it in on the 2026 season and building for the future.
That’s not the case, says Bijan Robinson .
“I know people outside of here think that we’re just plummeting the season,” Robinson told reporters on Wednesday. “Nah man, we’re focusing on this week, going to take it one game at a time, and go from there. Try to make a push; that’s where we’re at right now.”
Robinson said head coach Kevin Stefanski met with the Falcons’ leadership committee to ensure players remained on the same page and weren’t moping after the team’s trade-deadline moves. The running back said the committee took Stefanski’s message to heart and described the atmosphere inside Atlanta’s locker room as “positive.”
On Monday, a day after the 34-17 Madrid debacle against the Cincinnati Bengals , Atlanta made shocking moves to trade safety Jessie Bates III after four years with the team. Center Ryan Neuzil was moved on Tuesday in a buzzer-beating deal to the Baltimore Ravens.
For Bates, Atlanta got a 2027 NFL Draft second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder. In exchange for Neuzil, Atlanta received guard Andrew Vorhees and a 2028 sixth-round pick.
“We’re trying to win regardless, man,” Robinson said. “We understand that we got to make some moves, but it doesn’t [change] the fact that we’re still trying to get to where we want to get to in the season.”
Losing four of its last five, the Falcons look to be on a downward trend.
“I truly believe that we have the team and the guys that are going to rally and flip the script,” said quarterback Michael Penix Jr . “We got a lot of guys that care. Not just sitting here, sulking like, ‘We’re at 3-6 right now.’ We have to focus on what’s in front of us.”
But the fact of the matter is the Falcons are very much still in play for the NFC South divisional title, winning which would advance the franchise to the NFL playoffs for the first time since the 2017-2018 season.
Entering Week 10, Atlanta is a half game back from No. 1 in the NFC South, trailing the Carolina Panthers (3-5), New Orleans Saints (3-5), and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) in that order.
“We’re still in it,” Penix said. “We got an eight-game season left, and we really want to win all eight.”
But welcome to the NFC South, where you can simultaneously compete for the division crown and draft positioning. If the season ended today, the Falcons would have the 10th overall pick and pick Georgia linebacker Chris Cole, according to Tankathon .
The absurdity of taking a linebacker at No. 10 notwithstanding, the Falcons find themselves balancing two competing timelines: a front office making moves with the future in mind and a locker room still fighting for the present. Whether intentional or not, Atlanta’s trade-deadline decisions suggest a different direction from the one its players envision.
“That’s in no way a focus for me and us,” Stefanski said of Atlanta’s current draft standing. “We talk about long-term, short-term, but that’s not really a focus for us.”
Atlanta’s coming weeks are unrelenting.
This Sunday, Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) come to town. Then is the bye week.
Afterward, Atlanta will head to the Minnesota Vikings on Nov. 29 for the “Kirk Cousins Bowl,” then return home to face the Detroit Lions.
Whether the Falcons can turn their belief into wins remains to be seen. But with the front office already looking toward the future, the remaining schedule will test just how much this team has left to play for.
Falcons-Chiefs kicks off at 1 p.m. at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. CBS will air the game.

title: Falcons Teammates Confident DeMarcco Hellams Can Fill Jessie Bates’ Role
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are counting on DeMarcco Hellams to help fill the void left by Jessie Bates III, and his teammates believe the young safety is ready for the opportunity.
Atlanta traded Bates to the Jacksonville Jaguars ahead of the NFL trade deadline, receiving a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round selection in return. While losing a three-time All-Pro defender is a significant blow to the secondary, the Falcons now have an opportunity to evaluate what Hellams can bring in an expanded role.
“We understand the business of the game, the nature of the game. That leaves guys in position to step up, which is me,” Hellams said. “I feel like I came into the league to take every day to prepare like a starter. And when my moment comes, to be ready for it.”
For Hellams, that moment has arrived. Through nine games this season, mostly on special teams, he has recorded 14 total tackles, including five solo tackles and nine assists. He also has one pass deflection and one tackle for loss.
The fourth-year safety has spent much of his career working behind established players in Atlanta’s secondary. Now, he has an opportunity to show that he can handle a starting role.
Hellams has the support of his teammates, including rookie safety Xavier Watts, who expressed confidence in his ability to step into the vacant position.
“I think ’Marco (Hellams) is going to come in and do a great job. Jammie Robinson, a couple other guys who might kind of bounce around in that position. But, next-man-up mentality,” Watts said.
Jammie Robinson, Sydney Brown, and Billy Bowman Jr. provide additional depth and flexibility in the secondary.
Head coach Kevin Stefanski has also expressed confidence in Hellams, identifying him as the next man up.
“DeMarcco is the next man up that we feel really good about,” Stefanski said. “He has played good football for us.”
Replacing Bates’ production and leadership will not be an easy task. However, Atlanta does not need Hellams to become Bates overnight. The Falcons need him to play confidently, communicate effectively and help stabilize the back end of the defense.
His first test will be a big one. Patrick Mahomes, Travis Kelce, and the Kansas City Chiefs will put a lot of stress on the perimeter of the defense with their ability to extend plays.
For Hellams, this is an opportunity he has spent years preparing for. Now, with the starting job within reach, he has a chance to prove his teammates and coaches right.

title: Ryan Neuzil Trade Leaves Falcons With a Big Question on the Offensive Line
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons are 3-6, and they say the playoffs are still in reach. By Tuesday night, they had traded the center who started their last 26 games. On Sunday, his replacement will line up against Chris Jones.
Atlanta surprised many by trading center Ryan Neuzil at the deadline on Tuesday, flipping him to the Baltimore Ravens for interior offensive lineman Andrew Vorhees and a conditional 2028 draft selection.
Neuzil played five seasons with the Falcons and started the last 26 games (39 total). He was a solid center for Atlanta this season, allowing one sack and committing a single penalty, but the move makes it clear the team was ready to go in a different direction once he hit free agency this offseason.
In his place, Corey Levin will get the nod on Sunday.
“Obviously, love ‘Neuz’ [Ryan Neuzil],” Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski said Wednesday when asked about the move. “Great person. Just felt like this was an opportunity for our football team and comfortable and feel good about Corey Levin stepping in.”
Levin joined the Falcons this offseason, following his former offensive line coach, Bill Callahan, from the Tennessee Titans. He has mostly handled special teams for the Falcons this season, but that will ramp up in the second half.
Stefanski expressed confidence in Levin’s ability to step in, perform snaps with Michael Penix Jr., and hold up as the team’s starter. The head coach confirmed that Levin had already been getting reps in practice and would be ready to go. Stefanski said he feels “really good” about where Levin is in understanding what the team is doing.
“He brings great energy into the locker room and onto the field,” Falcons running back Bijan Robinson said about his new center. “He doesn’t have an off switch. He’s already ready to go, always ready to play, no matter what the situation is. He just gives extreme effort.”
But the veteran has started only three games since the end of the 2022 season, and what’s waiting for him on Sunday would be a difficult challenge for even the most tenured center. For the Falcons, it is a massive question mark that could leave the heart of the offense exposed.
The Kansas Chiefs piled on five sacks and pressured Jets quarterback Geno Smith on half of his dropbacks. Defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo is renowned for his ability to send exotic looks at players, and All-Pro defensive tackle Chris Jones recorded two of those sacks last Sunday – Levin will be matched up with him on every snap.
“Corey Levin, being a veteran center and a guy who’s played in games and can think the game,” Stefanski said, “is important for a week like this.”
The Falcons are banking on it, especially given how he's the only rostered player with starts at center.
As for the additional piece of the deal, the Falcons are confident in what they have in Vorhees.
The interior offensive lineman was a projected day-two pick in 2023, but a torn ACL during the scouting combine tanked him into the seventh round. He started all 20 games from 2024-25, and made five more appearances (two starts) this season.
In Atlanta, he will likely fill a depth guard position alongside Kyle Hinton. At 6-foot-6 and 330 pounds, Vorhees adds immediate interior size and the traits Callahan loves.
“I've competed against him over the years, and he's a good football player,” Stefanski said about the plan for Vorhees. “Coach [Bill] Callahan and crew will get their arms around him and get him up to speed.”
Vorhees will be a free agent this offseason, so there is no guaranteed future even if he pans out as a player the Falcons can develop over the final weeks of the season.
The playoffs are still in reach for this team , especially in a winnable NFC South, but the deadline moves didn't get them any closer. If anything, they’re further away.
They moved two starters , and the question shifts to why the team felt so comfortable leaving an important position in question with half the season still to play. It’s a reasonable question, given how the Falcons dropped to 3-6 on Sunday, their fourth loss in the last five games, but Stefanski reiterated that the focus has not shifted in this locker room.
“We’re excited about the opportunities we have in front of us, but decisions that are made for our football team are always in the best interest of our football team,” Stefanski said. “We talked about it earlier this week – sometimes there is that tension [between] short-term and long-term, but I know the group we have of players. I know the group we have of coaches and staff. Our focus hasn't changed one bit.”
The Falcons’ center position might say otherwise, and Chris Jones will test it on the first snap.
