title: Jaguars Mailbag: How the Dust Has Settled in Duval After Wild Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The dust has settled from the NFL Trade Deadline, and the Jacksonville Jaguars are set to be back on the field in just a few days.
The Jaguars are set to visit the Tennessee Titans in Week 10, and there is certainly a buzz around the game after the Jaguars' busy week of trades, even with Jessie Bates III and Jordan Davis set to miss the game.
In this week's Jaguars mailbag, we take a look at the fallout from the trades, what is ahead for the team, and much more.
Re: Godchaux Trade Did the Jags give up a 2026 or 2027 6th round pick? pic.twitter.com/sejPorIAPR
A: It is honestly a really interesting trade because I am not sure I have ever seen this kind of condition in a trade? It is a 2028 6th-round pick if the Jaguars do not end up getting a 2027 6th-round pick ... but the Jaguars are expected to get a sixth-round pick in the compensatory draft pick formula before next April. So, it is bascially going to be a sixth-round pick.
Do you think without D-Ham going down for the season they still make as big a splash as they did with Davis for say an Edge or true 3T DT, or did they just happen to find their player due to the injury need and who was actually made available aligning?
A: This is my take, and it is just a gut take: I think we can now say that the Jaguars were never going to leave this year's deadline with their first-round pick. They crave the trades. They yearn for the trades. Their stance is that they value picks, because it can help them year-round. They have made 12 trades not counting draft-day trades since the start of 2025. I think they were going to make a blockbuster even before the Davon Hamilton deal, though I am sure that still played a factor.
Everyone says Jordan Davis is a big-time run stuffer. And while that was his primary job in Philly, doesn't he possess pass rush abilities that could be just as needed in the interior?
A: There are a few layers to this. The way the Eagles used Davis was certainly as an early-down player. He was asked to hold the line of scrimmage and two-gap and react to blocks than he was asked to simply get upfield. With that said, he also did have his fair share of snaps at three-technique with the Eagles. There were chances for him to cash-in on production as a pass-rusher, and he did take advantage of those chances during his breakout 2025 season. I do think Davis has plenty of physical traits to suggest he has not yet had his talent tapped into. I think the Jaguars will let him play on more third downs than the Eagles did, though, which could be what he really needs. The Jaguars need him and BJ Green to make an impact there.
Now is anything missing from the Jags roster?
I think every team still has weaknesses. There is no juggernaut with a flawless team this year, though the Jaguars are maybe the closest thing through nine weeks. The Jaguars' offensive line has played mostly-well as a unit, but it will be a group that continues to get tested. They play a few disruptive edge rushers over the next three weeks before Jeffery Simmons after that, which should give us a barometer of where they are really at.
how does the addition of Jessie Bates change the likelihood of keeping Parker? and which player is a better candidate for the franchise tag if it comes to that?
I don't think it changes it that much, honestly. The Jaguars have been in the business of keeping their core pieces since the start of the 2025 offseason, and I think Washington is one of those pieces like Travon Walker was last season, and others before him. There are a few other guys who I could see walking, but Washington is not one of them. It would be more expensive to do for Washington, which could give them even more motivation to get him signed in the event they have to tag Jessie Bates.
Who is the 3rd safety now when Bates and Johnson are active: Merriweather or Lane? Will Huskey return to being inactive each week?
I think Rayuan Lane, who I believe is going to start against the Tennessee Titans on Sunday now that we know Jessie Bates isn't going to play . Lane has done some good things for the Jaguars this season and they certainly view him as more than just a special teams player. I think once Bates is in the lineup, the safety depth chart will have Lane at the No. 3 spot, Kaevon Merriweather at the No. 4 spot, and Jalen Huskey likely inactive like he was earlier in the season. This room has played well since the injuries hit, and they deserve another week in the sun in Week 10.
What's the transition period for Bates to fully understand the playbook/make calls in the backend. He's known as one of the smartest players in the NFL, but when would he be comfortable enough to translate what he sees, with his years of experience, to the other, younger DBs?
I think we will see Bates step into that kind of role very quickly. It might not take much time for him to step up as the true leader and voice of the unit; Jakobi Meyers made an impression at wide receiver in that same fashion a year ago. I think we will see his impact made on the rest of the younger secondary as early as Week 11 against the New York Giants.
Can Godchaux and Davis play DT at the same time, sparing some Armstead early down reps with the hope that he’s more efficient as a pass rusher? If not, how do you see the DT rotation playing out? Maybe Godchaux gets some reps against the run to give Davis some on 3rd down?
I absolutely think so. I think both guys can play both three-technique and nose tackle in the Jaguars' defense on early downs, something the Jaguars have done with their defensive tackles even before the Davon Hamilton injury. I think you will see Davis and Godchaux lead the way at the nose tackle spot, but they can also use them interchangbly with Arik Armstead, Ruke Orhorhoro, and Matt Dickerson.
Aside from an injury, what could derail the team from a deep playoff run? I would say the play of the CBs not named Travis Hunter; what about you?
A: The offensive line against an elite front. Them against the Denver Broncos' front would be a ... matchup to watch.
Let’s say the Jags make the playoffs and get a high seed. Who’s the one wildcard team you don’t want to see and why is it the Texans?
I would take the Jaguars against any of the other teams in the AFC right now. I think my answer though is Buffalo, just because of Josh Allen and what he can do to a team when he gets on a roll like he did a year ago. Houston is close due to CJ Stroud and a defense that I believe is still talented. The Bengals and Broncos are on the same tier, but for opposite reasons. The Bengals have a great offense but I think the Jaguars can get after their defense. The Broncos have a great defense, but I think the Jaguars can get after their offense.
Who do you think the Jags will let walk in free agency to keep their compensatory strategy going this offseason?
A: I think Arik Armstead and Ezra Cleveland are the locks. Davon Hamilton is one to at least consider with the future of the nose tackle spot clearly being spearheaded by Jordan Davis moving forward. Antonio Johnson and Ventrell Miller are two I am torn on. I could see them coming back like Montaric Brown did, but it might depend on the price tag.
Is there any realistic scenario where Camp stays?
Realistic? Sure. I think Anthony Campanile has deserved a shot to be one of the league's top head coach candidates in 2027 no matter how the rest of this season plays out. I also think teams are so into the mindset of hiring offensive coaches that I am not sure if there will be the perfect fit for Campanile quite yet. I think there is a chance he stays because of this reason, while I think the odds are smaller for offensive coordinator Grant Udinski. For example, I do not agree with it but it feels like the New York Jets would be hard-pressed to hire another first-year head coach with a defensive background after the Saleh-Glenn back-to-back attempts.
What will it take for the media to realize that Gladstone isn’t going…

title: Why the Jaguars Are Making the Right Call Slow-Playing the Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates Debuts
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars will have to wait one more week for the debuts of Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III.
"Jesse Bates and Jordan Davis will not play on Sunday due to not having a bye," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said on Friday.
"With their workload and the way the season falls from a scheduling standpoint, we want to be able to make sure that we're in player safety, putting them in a position to succeed. Also, learn the system, and just give those guys a week to be able to do that. So neither one will be playing on Sunday."
Not having either of their new pieces in Week 10 against the Tennessee Titans means their debuts will come in Week 11 against the New York Giants, and there are plenty of reasons why the Jaguars look to be making the right moves.
With the way the Jaguars are set to deploy Davon Godchaux in Week 10 against the Titans, it is clear the Jaguars are making this move based simply on the bye weeks. Godchaux got his bye week with the New Orleans Saints in Week 8, while Davis and Bates have each already played nine games this season. This trend goes back to last year, too, when the Jaguars made in-season trades for cornerback Greg Newsome and for wide receiver Jakobi Meyers.
Newsome was traded to the Jaguars before Week 6, just five weeks into the season. He got his bye week when the Jaguars got theirs in Week 8 that season. Meanwhile, Meyers already had his bye week when his trade to the Jaguars was completed after Week 9, which meant he would not be playing an extra game despite the trade.
Davis and Bates have each had rest days during their first two practice days with the Jaguars, which was the first indication that neither might play in their first Jaguars game in Nashville. The Jaguars have thus slow-played their onboarding process compared to other players they have drafted in the past, but neither player is in the situations Newsome, Meyers, or Godchaux were in.
Asking two veteran players to play 18 games would have made little sense for the Jaguars. And if the Jaguars feel like they needed Davis and Bates to do so to beat the Titans in Week 10, that would have rung quite a few alarms. Jacksonville beat the Baltimore Ravens last week before making any of these trades, and they are 6-2 for a reason. They would have been one of the best teams in the AFC regardless of their trade deadline moves, so this doesn't change much for them considering it is likely to be just for a week.
The Jaguars are of course not taking the Titans lightly by not playing Bates and Davis, because they would almost positively be sitting them if they were playing the Buffalo Bills or Denver Broncos in Week 10. But the Jaguars are taking a big-picture view with their new pieces. They will need them more in January than they will need them to beat Cam Ward, Robert Saleh, and Tony Pollard on Sunday.
Teams do not often complete blockbusters without the expectation of immediate impact and production. The Jaguars are comfortable with that impact coming in Week 11 against the New York Giants instead of this Sunday, and it feels like the right and mature decision.

title: Hopes for a Jaguars' Pass-Rush Boost Now Rest on BJ Green After Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars may not have added to their defensive end room during the trade deadline, but they are getting some reinforcements anyways.
The Jaguars opened the practice window for injured second-year defensive end BJ Green II this week, and Green has since been a full participant in back-to-back practices leading up to Week 10 against the Tennessee Titans , and it seems like there is a good chance he will be back on the field after his Week 1 injury.
After a trade deadline in which the Jaguars did not address the defensive end position during their defensive overhaul, the return of Green is the closest thing the Jaguars will get to reinforcements for their mid-season pass-rush. How big of an impact can Green make in that return, exactly?
The Jaguars' pass-rush and ability to impact the quarterback as a whole has been better than given credit for during their 6-2 run at the start of the season. The Jaguars do rank No. 25 in sacks and No. 19 in sack rate, but they are a top-eight team in terms of pressure rate due to how they create pressure. 22 different players have created a pressure for the Jaguars this year, a higher number than most defenses. From linebackers to cornerbacks to safeties, everyone on the defense is a part of the pass-rush.
But with the Jaguars making a serious push to be the AFC's best team over the second-half of the season, the team could stand to reason to look for improvements everywhere. They found improvements at safety with Jessie Bates III and at defensive tackle with Jordan Davis and Davon Godchaux. Now, they will need Green to offer some kind of boost to a defensive end room that is headlined by Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker and platooned by Danny Striggow and Bryan Thomas Jr.
Striggow and Thomas have been the primary backups in the defensive end rotation since Green's injury, with the two combining for 231 snaps over the first eight games, which amounts to nearly 29 snaps per game in which the Jaguars needs their depth. That means Green could make a serious impact if he is back at the top of the depth chart behind Hines-Allen and Walker like he was entering the season.
BJ Green with a big-time hit/sack on Justin Herbert. He’s somehow called for roughing the passer. pic.twitter.com/X2qkBCRwt6
Green, who had two sacks last year as a rookie, had a breakout training camp and looked bount to be a key piece of the Jaguars' rotation behind their star defensive ends. His injury felt like a blow to their defensive and special teams depth at the time, and now we can see what kind of impact he can make in his second season.
“I think he could be a big boost. B.J.'s got a lot of explosive qualities. I thought when he came in, and he came in, started playing for us right about this time last year," Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said Thursday.
"So obviously, battling the injury from early in the season, he's kind of going to be stepping in that same window. And I think he can give us a boost because he's an explosive guy. I think B.J. sets an edge, is physical and all that, those elements of the early down defense, but is really a good pass rusher and gives us some transition rush. So, he's got some skills that we definitely covet here, that's why he's been here and we're excited to get him back.”
The Jaguars have a talented defensive line that has played a big part in getting the team to 6-2 this season and 19-6 over the last two seasons combined. The Jaguars play a specific brand of football on the defensive side that sometimes aims for the quarterback to get the ball out of their hand quickly as a purposeful strategy, and it has worked for them.
But so many Super Bowl winners have had four-man rushes that can terrify opposing offenses. The Jaguars have the same capability, and Green's return could even provide a mid-season spark to let the numbers start pouring in. That is the hope, at least. Because no other help is coming.

title: Jaguars-Titans Injury Report: Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates Debuts Come With a Question
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars will be ready for their newest faces on defense to hit the ground running once they are settled in ... but will they be ready in Week 10?
The Jaguars' second injury report of Week 10 had new faces Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates as non-participants in practice for the second day in a row, with each player getting back-to-back rest days after the explosive trades that brought them to Jacksonville.
Davis and Bates each spoken to the media this week, with Davis saying "I'm here to do whatever the coaches need me to do," when asked about playing on Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. Bates said he still has to "knock off the plane ride from Spain," after playing there in Week 9 for the Atlanta Falcons, though he also said "I'm ready for sure."
It is worth noting that neither Davis or Bates have had bye weeks to this point, while the Jaguars have already had their bye week in Week 7. If Bates and Davis were to play every game for the Jaguars the rest of the way, each will have played 18 games in the regular-season, which doesn't even account for the likely playoff games that will come later.
There is also the adjustment period in general. Each Davis and Bates are getting crash courses in defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile's scheme, and both will have to be ready to execute at a high level if they are called upon this Sunday.
"I always feel like this, whenever you get a new guy in it’s more just getting the verbiage and everything down. Because that’s really what slows everything down for you," Campanile said on Thursday.
"Once you've got the verbiage and you understand what everything means, I think in every building there are probably a lot of similarities. Things that everybody does, they've all done before, but it's just translating it, and how fast you can get that across to the players and they feel comfortable with it. They can just line up and go play. If you're going out there and you're thinking, it’s super hard to have all your skills, so we're working on getting them to that point right now.”
There does not appear to be as much mystery with fellow new Jaguars defender Davon Godchaux, who the Jaguars acquired from the New Orleans Saints for a conditional future sixth-round pick. Godchaux has practiced for the Jaguars in back-to-back days, which could indicate he makes his debut sooner than Davis and Bates do.
Meanwhile, the Jaguars did have one player who did not participate due to injury: running back Bhayshul Tuten, who has not practiced since sustaining an ankle/foot injury in Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts.
Tuten ended up playing against the Baltimore Ravens on a short week last week despite not practicing, rushing 12 times for 29 yards and a touchdown while playing a season-low 35.7% of the offensive snaps.
"I think first and foremost, it speaks to his toughness to be able to go out there and do that on a short week. It's tough enough as it is to go out and play on that short week," Jaguars offensive coordinator Grant Udinski said on Thursday.
"It's such a quick turnaround for those guys no matter what position you're at, but he's been carrying the load for us and to turn around and do that is super impressive and it's a credit to him and his values that he places on the team. Kind of a selfless act to be out there and try to give it his best when he might not be 100%.

title: How the NFL Trade Deadline Changed the Jaguars' Defensive Depth Chart
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars defense has a few new faces after the trade deadline, and they should be expected to play roles very, very quickly.
Few people in Jacksonville should be as excited about the Jaguars' massive new pieces as new defensive cooridnator Anthony Campanile ... for obvious reasons.
“Obviously really fired up about it. Any time you get three great players and three great people in the building… So, I couldn’t be more excited about it," Campanile said on Thursday.
"The team itself I think feels the exact same way. They’ve kind of hit the ground running, our three new guys, three new teammates. They’re working really hard, working tirelessly; I can say that. They’ve been in here putting in hours trying to get acclimated and they’ve been everything everyone said they were in terms of the types of guys they are.”
So, what does the Jaguars' defensive depth chart look like now after adding multiple starters? We break it down below.
Starters: Josh Hines-Allen, Travon Walker
Backups: Danny Striggow-Bryan Thomas Jr.-BJ Green II-Wesley Williams
The Jaguars added to quite a few spots over the course of the trade deadline, but the defensive end spot is one that there is no new face. Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen are still set to lead the defensive end room, while the Jaguars are set to get BJ Green back from injured reserve sooner than later after they opened his practice window earlier this week. This was a big area of focus ahead of the trade deadline, but the Jaguars are what they are at the spot.
It is clear that Danny Striggow is the No. 3 EDGE and that rookie Wesley Williams is set to contiue to be a healthy scratch. If Green is able to hit the ground running after his injury, then he should be taking a leap over Thomas on the depth chart over the next few weeks. Other than that, this depth chart is as is.
Starters: Arik Armstead, Jordan Davis
Backups: Davon Godchaux-Matt Dickerson-Ruke Orhorhoro-Albert Regis
This is the big change. The Jaguars added two big pieces to the defensive line with Jordan Davis and Davon Godchaux, and they should be expected to play massive roles from the jump. Davis should be able to step right into the Jaguars' nose tackle role after Davon Hamilton's injury, and the Jaguars have a lot of confidence in his ability to contribute as a pass-rusher and not just a run-stuffer.
Behind Davis and Armstead, the Jaguars have some good depth. Godchaux can give them strong snaps as a rotational nose tackle, Matt Dickerson can give them a boost as a nose tackle and three-technique on run downs, while Ruke Orhorhoro is potentially their second-best interior pass-rusher. This is a much, much-improved group.
Starters: Foyesade Oluokun, Ventrell Miller, Dennis Gardeck
Backups: Branson Combs-Jahlani Tavai-Jalen McLeod
The Jaguars are ho-hum at the linebacker room. Ventrell Miller and Foyesade Oluokun  are one of the best linebacker duos in the NFL in terms of pure production. Jacksonville has played the linebacker position perfectly in terms of adding to the room over the years, and the decision to make Ventrell Miller the starter and letting Devin Lloyd walk in free agency.
Starters: Travis Hunter, Montaric Brown, Jourdan Lewis
Backups: Jarrian Jones-Jaylon Jones
The Jaguars are set to have their same cornerback room after the trade deadline, but the entire secondary should be impacted by the Jessie Bates move. I think it is also clear that Jarrian Jones is closer to being a starter than he is a true backup, but there are still only so many players who can be listed as starters. With the Jaguars moves, though, this is a strong room from No. 1 to No. 4.
Starters: Jessie Bates III, Antonio Johnson
Backups: Rayuan Lane-Kaevon Merriweather-Jalen Huskey
This is where some real change has happened. The Jaguars did not trade a second- and fifth-round pick to Atlanta for Bates to not be a starter the second he has been caught up to speed. The more interesting question is what happens on the other spots of the depth chart at safety behind Bates and fellow starter Antonio Johnson. The Jaguars saw Rayuan Lane step in as their No. 2 safety after Eric Murray's injury, so he figures to be the most likely option at the No. 3 spot.
The Jaguars have also used Kaevon Merriweather as a top backup at safety, but he looks like he will most likely be a special teamer moving forward. As for rookie Jalen Huskey, he has been a healthy scratch for most of the season and that will likely be where he is at for game day moving forward throughout the rest of the season.

title: 3 Biggest Questions Facing the Jaguars After Trade Deadline Fallout: Is the Pass-Rush Enough?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars got better over the trade deadline. In their estimation, they got a lot better.
But even after the Jaguars added some big pieces in the form of Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates III, and Davon Godchaux, there are still questions facing the team as they make their playoff run down the stretch of 2026.
So, what are the biggest questions facing the Jaguars after James Gladstone's trade deadline fireworks? We break it down below.
The Jaguars had three big needs entering the trade deadline : adding help at defensive tackle, safety, and defensive end. The Jaguars certainly checked two of those boxes, with the additions of Davis, Godchaux and Bates expected to make a significant impact right out of the gate. But while the Jaguars did improve their run defense and play-making ability in the secondary, the Jaguars made no moves at defensive end, aside from opening the practice window for second-year defensive end BJ Green off injured reserve.
Jacksonville could see more of a pass-rush upside in Davis than he saw in Philadelphia, where he recorded 9.5 sacks in over 70 games. Davis played in a similar scheme with the Eagles than he will with the Jaguars, so this seems like more of a bet in traits than past production. The Jaguars have been able to generate pressure at a consistent rate all year without a true interior pass-rusher, largely due to their pressure packages and extra blitzers, but there could be a question as to whether the Jaguars' four-man pass-rush is good enough once January comes around.
The Jaguars reportedly were interested in Jets pass-rusher Will McDonald IV, which could imply that they are aware of this need as well. Despite not a ton of sack production over two years, though, the Jaguars have still had a top-rated defense and have won far more often than they have lost. Perhaps that continues now.
The addition of Bates to the back end of the Jaguars' defense will obviously have a lasting impact on the room, with the future looking murky in terms of Eric Murray returning next season. Caleb Ransaw and Jalen Huskey are third-round picks who have not played all that much, which means the future of the safety room right now has to center around Bates and Antonio Johnson. The issue, of course, is that both safeties are in contract years, and the Jaguars now may have to determine which one they bring back.
Perhaps the Jaguars are able to keep both safeties, but you do not see teams drop big deals for multiple safeties in one offseason all that often. The Jaguars could also let one walk and hope to get a compensatory pick back in return after free-agency and then hope that Ransaw, Huskey, or Rayuan Lane are ready to step into the second safety spot.
It is a tough question to weigh. The Jaguars gave up a big trade package to land Bates, who is a ready-made All-Pro safety and is one of the best in the NFL. Letting him walk would seem misguided. On the other hand, Johnson is one of the best young players on one of the NFL's oldest defenses, and he has developed each year under this regime. This could be a tough balance.
The Jaguars opted not to trade Brian Thomas Jr. at the trade deadline, which makes sense considering the Jaguars are in a position to add talent to the roster, not take it away. But the onus is now on the Jaguars to prove that they made the right decision to not use Thomas and his decreasing role on offense as a way to recoup some of the draft picks they dealt over the trade deadline period. Thomas is a real-deal talent, but the Jaguars took a risk by opting to keep him for the rest of the 2026 season.
When it comes to that risk, the Jaguars are also largely the ones who can make it pay off or not. Thomas will have to be at his best when the ball comes his way, which has not always been the case over the last two seasons, but the Jaguars also have to give him chances to make an impact. He hasn't had many of those chances this season, and now the Jaguars must make good on their decision to keep him by increasing those opportunities.

title: Should the Chiefs Reunite with Hollywood Brown?
full_text:
Even though the Kansas City Chiefs acquired wide receiver Josh Downs just before the NFL trade deadline, the team's wide receiver depth chart still has room for more talent. Could a familiar face be the next addition? It's complicated.
On Thursday, the Philadelphia Eagles released wide receiver Marquise "Hollywood" Brown after a disappointing few months in Philly. He caught only five passes for 63 yards in four games with the Eagles. That pales in comparison to his 49-catch, 587-yard, five-touchdown season with the Chiefs in 2025. The Eagles have had an avalanche of issues this season, but Brown never found his role in Philadelphia.
Certainly, Brown isn't at the top of his game, but in his age-29 season, he also isn't beyond a potential resurgence in a reasonable role. So, should the Chiefs and Brown be viewing each other as solutions to the other's problem? Let's look at the pros and cons.
With Tyquan Thornton on injured reserve for the forseeable future , the Chiefs still lack a proven deep threat who can stretch opposing defenses and present a plausible target for a couple of deep shot attempts per game. Xavier Worthy has the requisite speed to stretch the field, but he's never seemed entirely comfortable or productive in that role.
Meanwhile, Brown wouldn't (and shouldn't) impact Downs' role in any way. Downs will step in as a short- and intermediate-level threat who can separate against man-to-man coverage; Brown would be doing an entirely different job if he were to return.
The biggest feather in Brown's cap is his familiarity with the Chiefs' offense. When Andy Reid discussed potential receiver additions before the deadline, he began by saying that he'd "hope they'd be familiar with the offense." Brown certainly is, after spending two years in Kansas City before his brief time in Philly. If the Chiefs have interest in adding another pass-catcher who should be comfortable in the system, Brown would check that box.
Andy Reid shares what he'd look for in a potential addition at WR: “You'd hope they'd be familiar with the offense. If they're not, they gotta be smart and be able to pick it up quickly — I've had players that have done that and done it well, but I would tell you there better be… pic.twitter.com/xvBMCkrwxo
While the Chiefs would certainly value Brown's familiarity with the offense, would Brown be excited to sign with the Chiefs for a third time after an up-and-down 2025 campaign? Teams like the Steelers and 49ers, also often rumored to be in the receiver market, may have a more direct role for Brown as opposed to a deep-threat-and-depth position with the Chiefs.
From Kansas City's perspective, signing Brown would likely add another layer of insulation in front of rookie Cyrus Allen, whose regular season production hasn't yet lived up to his training camp hype. (It could also lead to a demotion for Worthy, who has led the receivers in snaps taken this year by a wide margin.) Do the Chiefs see room for late-season growth from Allen, or have they retained their optimism for Worthy's role in his third year? If so, adding Brown as the team's fourth or fifth receiver might not make sense for either side.
Another hypothetical to monitor: Are the Chiefs still keeping a door open for Tyreek Hill's potential return? In a battle of veteran receivers who are familiar with the offense, I would guess that the Chiefs would have more interest in the 32-year-old Hill, though his health and potential league-discipline status are both publicly unknown as of mid-November. I don't think the team is likely to invite both Hill and Brown back to Kansas City, ultimately adding three receivers during the middle of the season.
The Chiefs could pass on both free agent vets, but if they sign one, I wouldn't expect to see the other back in red.
Given the number of snaps that have recently been allocated to receivers like Jalen Royals and Andrew Armstrong, and with the practice squad addition of Justin Watson , I couldn't be upset with a return to Kansas City for Brown. Even in the midst of an entirely disappointing year that began with the Eagles, capable NFL receivers are hard to come by, and players with comfort in Reid's offense are even more valued.
Still, if the Chiefs think that the new duo of Downs and Rashee Rice is enough to lead the way alongside Travis Kelce, with Worthy as the deep threat and Allen waiting in the wings as the next man up, I wouldn't begrudge them for passing up on this reunion.

title: Kenneth Walker’s Status for Chiefs-Falcons Clash in Jeopardy With Concerning Injury
full_text:
Two days before the Kansas City Chiefs kick off their road tilt with the Falcons , they received some extremely concerning news on the injury front this afternoon.
During Andy Reid's media availability, he revealed that star running back Kenneth Walker III is dealing with a groin injury. As a result, Walker did not participate in Friday's practice session and could be designated as questionable leading up to the matchup. "Kenneth Walker came in this morning and had a tight groin, so we just sat him out of practice," Reid told reporters today. "We'll see how he feels this afternoon with rehab and through tomorrow."
Kenneth Walker didn't practice Friday because of a tight groin.
Reid explained that Walker informed the coaching staff in the morning that he had tweaked something and needed to get checked out. He also noted that Walker isn't the kind of player to sit out unless something is really bothering him.
The former Seahawks tailback has been sensational in his first year in Kansas City , leading the NFL in rushing yards per game and amassing over 1,000 yards from scrimmage and 11 total touchdowns across eight appearances. However, there appears to be a chance he is absent from the lineup this Sunday. Walker was always considered an injury-prone player in Seattle, though his only scare with the Chiefs before this one was a minor ankle ailment that forced him to miss the preseason finale . The 2025 campaign marked the first time in his career that he was able to suit up for all 17 games.
If the highly anticipated ground game battle between Walker and Bijan Robinson doesn't take place, fifth-round rookie Emmett Johnson will make his first NFL start in the backfield. Reid said that he would be the next Chief in line for carries and expressed confidence in his ability.
The Nebraska product has been remarkably productive lately , as he's totaled 177 yards from scrimmage and two touchdowns on just 12 touches over the past two weeks. He is a dynamic rusher who ranks among the NFL's best at forcing missed tackles, even with limited opportunities.
Aside from Johnson, Kansas City's running back depth is dangerously thin. Brashard Smith is currently on injured reserve, while third-string Jadyn Ott is questionable for Sunday's contest with a hamstring injury. Should he and Walker not be available this weekend, the Chiefs will only have one active ball carrier on the roster before making any corresponding moves.
Because of how late Walker popped up on the injury radar, it's difficult to say what his outlook is for KC's Week 10 matchup, but initial indications certainly aren't too promising. Reid did not disclose whether Walker's groin started tightening up recently or whether he had been battling through it for some time.
Fans should soon find out more about the severity of this injury and whether he can take the field at Mercedes-Benz Stadium.

title: ESPN Matchup Predictor Analyzes Chiefs vs. Falcons Showdown in Week 10
full_text:
After making a statement at Arrowhead Stadium, the Kansas City Chiefs will head back out on the road in Week 10 as the hosting Atlanta Falcons will attempt to play spoiler. KC is looking to build on its blowout win over the Jets in its previous outing.
The Falcons have lost four of their past five matchups but aren't technically out of it given the dire state of the NFC South. As a result, Kevin Stefanski's group is viewing this contest as a must-win if they want to stay in the playoff race. Despite Kansas City's impressive 6-2 record, Andy Reid and Co. have dealt with special teams struggles and offensive inconsistencies. Those issues have put a damper on what has otherwise been a successful start.
Most analysts view the Chiefs as heavy favorites, but what does the ESPN Matchup Predictor forecast? Here's what the computer model expects two days before kickoff.
ESPN Matchup Predictor Chances at Victory: Chiefs 78.1%, Falcons 21.6%.
With nearly a four-in-five chance of coming out victorious, the matchup predictor heavily favors Kansas City this weekend.
Chiefs fans can only take things one week at a time. Until the Broncos lose and give Kansas City an opening, all the Chiefs can do is beat the opponents in front of them.
The biggest storyline of this road clash is the arrival of Josh Downs , who landed with the Chiefs shortly before the trade deadline passed. The shifty slot receiver may not be featured too much out of the gate due to his unfamiliarity with the playbook, but there are bound to be some bright spots in his debut in the red and gold.
Kenneth Walker III is a dynamic weapon in the backfield , but Bijan Robinson is on another level. In spite of poor quarterback play, Robinson is virtually unstoppable in the open field and possesses elite vision as a runner. He has three games in which he surpassed 100 yards this season and is averaging 5.2 yards per carry. Atlanta is unsurprisingly a significant underdog coming into this one, though it really depends on which version of the Falcons show up on Sunday. They were blown out by the Bengals last time out and shut out by the Buccaneers a week prior, but they also hold upset victories over the 49ers and Packers.
The drastic shifts in Atlanta's play have fans scratching their heads, largely due to the play of quarterback Michael Penix Jr. A week after taking home NFC Offensive Player of the Week honors in Week 7, he tossed a career-high four interceptions and failed to get his team a point.
Heading into their final game before a bye, the Falcons are going to throw everything they can at the visiting squad to stay in contention. This is the type of matchup that could see the Chiefs fall into an early deficit if they aren't careful.

title: Chiefs Week 10 Injury Report: Two Key Trenches Players Remain Absent From Practice
full_text:
While the Kansas City Chiefs handily defeated the New York Jets last Sunday, several offensive starters came away with injuries. There seemed to be a good chance that KC would be without several contributors for this week's matchup against the Falcons.
Patrick Mahomes (elbow/knee) and Xavier Worthy (hamstring) have fully participated in practice the past two days, suggesting they are trending toward playing. However, a pair of key players in the trenches are currently in danger of missing the Week 10 contest. Two Chiefs were listed as nonparticipants on Thursday's injury report , those players being right tackle Jaylon Moore and defensive tackle Peter Woods. All signs indicate they won't be cleared to return by Sunday.
Amid the messy Josh Simmons fiasco , Moore has been thrust into a full-time role at right tackle while undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson mans the left side. The 28-year-old has started all but one game for the Chiefs this season, his only absence coming in Week 7 when he was in the NFL's concussion protocol .
Now, the veteran swing tackle is dealing with an ankle ailment that forced him to exit the Jets win in the second half. In his place, Joshua Ezeudu stepped in on the outside, and he could be in line for his second start as a Chief if Moore doesn't take part in Friday's practice session.
Meanwhile, rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods continues to work his way back from a neck stinger that has plagued him for nearly a month. It was not initially considered a long-term issue when he first sustained it , but he's now on track to miss his second consecutive week for KC.
Many Chiefs fans have eagerly awaited the return of Omarr Norman-Lott, the franchise's second-round draft pick last year. He tore his ACL in Week 7 of his rookie year and has been rehabbing back since. Kansas City designated him to return from the physically unable to perform (PUP) list on Oct. 28. The Chiefs have listed him as a limited participant on Wednesday and Thursday, signaling his long-awaited 2026 debut may be nearing. Regardless, time is running out for Norman-Lott to be activated before his 21-day practice window closes.
Although Norman-Lott does not technically need to return for the Chiefs' upcoming game, he only has until Nov. 18 to be added to the 53-man roster. Otherwise, he will revert to the reserve list permanently for the remainder of the year, closing any avenue for him to get back into game action.
Considering Woods is likely to be unavailable against Atlanta, Norman-Lott's presence would do a lot for the pass rush , which recently broke out with a five-sack outing versus New York.

title: Josh Downs’ Biggest Goal After Joining Chiefs Should Be Music to Fans’ Ears
full_text:
Whenever a team acquires a player at the NFL trade deadline , it always opens the door for exciting possibilities the rest of the way that season. It also presents an obstacle or two, however, and the Kansas City Chiefs have shown that as much as any club in recent years.
In reality, 2024 might be the most apt example of that. Wide receiver DeAndre Hopkins was heavily involved early on, only to see his production taper off over time, and defensive end Josh Uche never carved out a real role after coming over to his new organization. Kansas City-specific additions frequently encounter steep learning curves and adjustment periods.
The prized newcomer of 2026, wide receiver Josh Downs , is trying his best to ensure his transition is as seamless as possible.
As a short-area savant who operates primarily out of the slot, Downs figures to compete for some of the work tight end Travis Kelce and fellow wideout Rashee Rice are getting. That includes a variety of concepts and potential choice or option routes, giving the fourth-year man plenty to absorb as he enters a new system.
Heck, not quite having complete mastery of the offense is part of the reason why rookie Cyrus Allen's involvement has lagged behind the hype nine games into his Chiefs tenure. Can Downs catch on quicker and make a good impression with quarterback Patrick Mahomes?
Speaking to the media this week, he said that's what he's setting out to do.
"Build that relationship with him and then on the field, when he throws me the ball, just catch it," Downs said. "And keep making plays when he throws it to me. Just do anything I can to learn the offense as fast as possible. I don't want to be a guy that's asking everybody what the play is [or] what the formation is. I feel like that's when you kind of get left behind, so I want to do everything I can to learn as fast as possible."
Downs also opened up on going from the 2-7 Colts, who have already lost to Kansas City this season, to a 6-2 club that anticipates both qualifying for the postseason and making a run at the Super Bowl.
"It's great to join a team like this with so much history and so much winning in their past, and even now," Downs said. "So I'm excited to be able to be a part of a group like this and contribute where I can."
In three-and-a-half years as a Colt, Downs was targeted an even 350 times in the passing game and managed to log 231 receptions for 2,494 yards and 12 touchdowns. That came with a 66.0% catch rate and 50.6% success rate, although his sophomore effort may have been his best in totality. Downs was effective last year despite playing 6% fewer snaps than the campaign prior.
After requesting a trade and having that ask met by his old franchise, Downs has nothing but love for Indianapolis and is ready to hit the ground running for his new one.
"I know they made a decision based off the betterment of their organization," Downs said. "I respect them for sending me to an organization like this. Those are great people over there, and I feel like they did right by me. This is the choice they made."
If Downs can accomplish his goal and grasp the playbook with efficiency while also earning Mahomes' trust, both he and the Chiefs will be all the better for it.

title: What Does Chiefs’ Reported CB Trade Interest Before Deadline Say About the Secondary?
full_text:
The only trade the Kansas City Chiefs made at the deadline saw them acquire former Colts receiver Josh Downs to bolster the receiving corps. However, that wasn't the only position group Brett Veach hoped to improve on the open market.
According to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler , the Chiefs held substantial interest in adding a cornerback before Tuesday's deadline. While no deal came to fruition, it may have revealed how the front office views the defensive backfield and its confidence in the current personnel. In the last two games, KC has primarily operated with Nohl Williams and Kristian Fulton on the outside, mixing in Chris Roland-Wallace as the primary slot corner. That rotation would look significantly different if it weren't for the injuries to the secondary.
Although he has been a full participant in practice this week and is expected to return against the Falcons, Mansoor Delane's shoulder has has been a recurring problem all year long. He suffered a hairline fracture in his right shoulder blade during OTAs in the offseason, forcing him to wear a non-contact jersey throughout most of training camp. The LSU product reaggravated it in his NFL debut after coming down with an interception, and a setback in practice last month forced him to miss the past two contests .
The concern with Delane isn't how he's performed, as he's been quite effective during his rookie season. Despite having missed three games, he holds the highest Pro Football Focus defensive grade (79.7) among all NFL rookie cornerbacks, allowing just 14 receptions for 227 yards in coverage.
Still, it shouldn't come as a surprise that the Chiefs were exploring their options given the depleted state of their defensive backs. Since placing L'Jarius Sneed on injured reserve with a knee strain, Kansas City's pass defense has been compromised by a lack of continuity.
Fowler's report didn't provide much insight into the caliber of player the Chiefs were pursuing, but the lack of a move doesn't necessarily mean they are comfortable with their current group. It's possible the franchise views Delane's shoulder ailment as an ongoing question mark for the remainder of the season. Part of Kansas City's reluctance to overpay for a cornerback could be attributed to Fulton's unexpected resurgence. While he was an afterthought coming off a lackluster first season in the red and gold, Fulton has surprisingly looked like a lockdown corner since being thrust into a bigger role this season.
Kristian Fulton has allowed just 50 receiving yards over 8 catches (15 targets) this season Qbs are registering a 32.6 passer rating when targeting KC's veteran CB
Having Fulton as a dependable depth piece has benefited KC tremendously. Regardless, the Chiefs may not have complete confidence in him as the secondary boundary cornerback starting in a playoff game should Delane's injury worsen at some point.
Williams has served as a stabilizing presence all year and has emerged as a real star in his second NFL season . The good news is that his strong play has helped offset concerns about Delane's availability.
Steve Spagnuolo is confident in the cornerbacks on his roster, and the Chiefs' interest in making an addition was probably more a product of their injury concerns than dissatisfaction with the players' performances. Either way, this group is only a season-ending injury away from being dangerously thin, and Kansas City didn't do anything at the deadline to provide insurance.

title: Chiefs’ Kicker Decision for Week 10 Is Bordering on Blind Faith
full_text:
With nine weeks of play and the NFL trade deadline in the books, the Kansas City Chiefs are in good standing overall but have some potential red flags. One of them is in a lesser-appreciated realm, but it could continue to loom large if not resolved in time for the postseason.
Head coach Andy Reid's squad and Dave Toub's special teams unit still can't rely on the kicking game to produce quality results. Longtime starter Harrison Butker's nightmare season rolled on in last weekend's win over the New York Jets, presumably making his seat even hotter with another subpar performance.
Is that actually the case, though? Despite former Pro Bowler Justin Tucker being ready to go on a moment's notice, KC has yet to make a swap at the position. Those expecting a changing of the guard on Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons will have to wait at least one more week.
Speaking to the media on Wednesday, Reid announced that he's trotting Butker out again in Week 10.
"As far as the kicking part goes, I'm going to stick with Butker this week," Reid said. "We'll go from there."
Reid and Toub have remained consistent in their backing of Butker , routinely pointing to his past accomplishments as justification for the unwavering faith. Instead of a new norm, the coaching staff is echoing that this is merely a cold spell of sorts.
"Listen, Harrison's done such a great job for us over time here," Reid said. "Sometimes, you go through these little peak and valley things. You give him a chance to work through them; we'll see how things go."
Another week of Butker highlights a multitude of concerns with the club's current approach to rectifying the ongoing kicking woes.
First and foremost, believing Butker is going to return to prime form borders on blind faith. The 31-year-old is perfectly fine on kicks inside the 50-yard line, going 10-for-11 on the year, but it's his long-range ability that — at least statistically — seems unlikely to come back.
After going 2-for-5 on field goals of 50-plus yards in 2024, he "rebounded" to post a 5-for-8 mark last season and is a career-worst 2-for-8 this year. In a sport where more and more kickers seem to be gaining either distance or accuracy, Kansas City's go-to man is losing both. This doesn't pass the smell test of someone who, in Reid's words , is "off a bit."
There's also the Tucker aspect of it all. If the Chiefs were so confident in a Butker resurgence, why would they bring in competition on the practice squad and keep him around for this long? That's on top of the reality that Tucker is in as a 36-year-old player who hasn't kicked in a game since the 2024 season and made only 73.3% of his tries, including converting on six of 11 attempts from that all-important long distance.
Maybe there is a world where Butker levels out. He found his stride, to some degree, in 2025-26 after a slow start out of the gate. Perhaps even if he doesn't, there's a concession from the coaching staff and Tucker proves to be closer to his 2023 self than the version we last saw. It's improbable, albeit not impossible.
But this comes off as a team hoping to catch lightning in a bottle rather than one that's truly getting to the bottom of a pressing issue.

title: Chiefs Winners and Losers After the Trade Deadline: Actually a New-Look WR Room?
full_text:
The unofficial second half of the 2026-27 NFL campaign is here, which coincides with the passing of the annual trade deadline . Several teams capitalized on opportunities to add to their respective rosters, with the Kansas City Chiefs being among the group of perceived winners.
By acquiring wide receiver Josh Downs from the Indianapolis Colts, Kansas City improved the route-running quality of its skill players while also maintaining some flexibility for the future. Whether the move can raise the upside of the offense or is worth the cost is another argument, but there's no denying that at least trying to get better was a good call in a vacuum.
In this post-deadline world, where do the Chiefs stand on an individual front? Let's dive into who should benefit from the move, as well as whose roles might be changed in negative ways.
The following players should benefit from the Downs trade by way of either increased production, decreased pressure, or both.
What better way to start than with the man himself? It feels like forever ago that the Colts' offense was viewed as football's best, but the reality is that was only a calendar year ago. Through 10 weeks of play in the 2025 campaign, per RBSDM , Indianapolis led the sport in EPA per play on that end (0.183) and was second to only the Los Angeles Rams in success rate.
Everyone knows what a horrific collapse Indianapolis had down the stretch, partially due to getting exposed but also because quarterback Daniel Jones tore his Achilles tendon. Despite Jones' return for the 2026-27 season, things still haven't gone even close to smoothly for head coach Shane Steichen's crew.
It's safe to say that going from catching passes from Jones to Patrick Mahomes could have a positive effect on the fourth-year wideout's prospects.
Josh Downs went from Daniel Jones to Patrick Mahomes - here is how they stack up in catchable aimed pass attempts in 2026 🎯 Catchable pass rate (rank of 29 QBs): 0-9 yds: Jones 83% (24th) → Mahomes 91% (2nd) 10-19: 59% (26th) → 68% (12th) 20+: 21% (29th) → 45% (17th) pic.twitter.com/acJg1HA8ai
Speaking of which, having another reliable pass catcher figures to come to Mahomes' aid as well. It's a two-way street.
Coming into the season, Kansas City was banking on several things to happen at the receiver spot. Not only did Xavier Worthy need to look more like he did as a rookie — or perhaps even better — but Rashee Rice was supposed to return to his pre-injury form and Tyquan Thornton was expected to take a step forward. It's safe to say that plan, which was on thin ice to begin with, hasn't worked.
If anything, Worthy has regressed and now has a bum hamstring . Rice sustained a hamstring injury of his own in Week 4 and isn't remotely as productive on a volume basis as he was last year. Thornton, who was actually living up to the hype, is done for most or all of this season with a dislocated ankle . Enter Downs, who now might be the best separator and technician Mahomes has had in years at the receiver position.
WR percentile separation & YPRR vs man coverage pic.twitter.com/NWbBKMMNRi
No. 15 has still managed to turn in a good season, throwing for 14 touchdowns and four interceptions, but his life's been much more difficult than is needed. This move should assist him on all downs and make the offense hum more efficiently as a result.
On a per-target basis, tight end Travis Kelce's been more effective in 2026 than he has in several years. He's producing a career-high 14.6 yards per reception and 10.0 yards per target, paired with an average of 10.0 yards after catch per reception. Kansas City isn't force-feeding him volume, instead allowing him to pick his spots while playing 4% fewer snaps than he was last season.
Had Kelce been at or near his peak involvement, he'd be a bit more of a loser than a winner with Downs coming to the Chiefs. Because his catches cut deeper this campaign, though, it's hard to not see him either maintaining his current output or reaching new heights in what could be the final stretch of his first-ballot Hall of Fame career.
The jury is out in the "losers" category, as the welcoming of Downs to the lineup likely changes some things moving forward.
After a slow start while recovering from offseason knee surgery , Rice went off for seven receptions and 88 yards in Week 3. Since returning from injury in Week 8, he's averaged six receptions and 51 yards across two games while also scoring a touchdown. Whatever momentum he had from a stat-sheet-stuffing standpoint may be slowing down with another peer to compete with, however.
Josh Downs averages 0.23 EPA/target this season, per @SumerSports Rashee Rice entered today with the highest EPA/target among Chiefs WRs at 0.15
Adding to the SumerSports data , Rice is 29th out of 111 wideouts with at least 100 routes at a 2.0 yards per route run mark. Downs is way down at 76th at 1.14, but that number is pretty deceiving given the injuries to the Colts' receiver unit and how inept the offense has been. If Downs gets the looks from Mahomes many are expecting, it means Rice's ceiling is capped.
There's also the element of these two thriving in similar areas of the field. According to Pro Football Focus , 46.7% of Rice's targets are coming within 0-9 yards of the line of scrimmage. That threshold is 61.5% for Downs.
After combining for 19 offensive snaps in his first five games, rookie fifth-rounder Cyrus Allen's figures were 16, 31 and 19 over his next three outings. Week 9 marked a regression for the former Cincinnati standout, unfortunately, as he fumbled on a kickoff return and also went without a catch on offense. Worthy's injury didn't see him get unleashed, either, so his stock was already down .
It's virtually impossible for a true breakout to happen as long as the trio of Rice, Downs and Worthy is healthy and available. Allen can still perhaps make a couple plays a game as a supporting piece, although that isn't the rest-of-season path some wanted him to take. Chalk that up to a classic tug-of-war between expectations and reality.
This one is unfortunate, but it's sometimes simply a numbers game when it comes to roster math. The Chiefs needed to make room for a better player, which meant special teams ace Nikko Remigio got the boot by way of being waived on Wednesday morning.
Remigio has several years of teams experience, on top of a thorough understanding of the offensive system, but it became clear when Rice was out in both 2025 and 2026 that he was never going to find an expanded role. Downs having his name added to the depth chart essentially signaled the complete extinguishment of those hopes for the former undrafted free agent.
Side note: Downs was spotted warming up with the punt team in Wednesday's practice. I'm still hard-pressed to believe he'll take many of Remigio's old reps, especially with this being more of a standard procedure during the week than anything else.
I struggled with where to put Worthy. While it seems likely that his overall workload and involvement in the offense will decline with Downs in the fold, it could take some pressure off him and make him a more impactful player overall. We'll wait and see.

title: Grading the Chiefs' Trade for Josh Downs: The Move KC Had to Make
full_text:
As the 2026 NFL trade deadline approached, everyone knew that the Kansas City Chiefs were in the market for wide receiver help . Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Josh Downs was the player most often mocked to Kansas City, even as other receivers were rumored to be on the market .
On Tuesday, only two wide receivers were actually traded, and they both came from Indianapolis. The Colts sent Keenan Allen to the San Francisco 49ers for a 2027 sixth-round pick, while the Chiefs added Downs (and a late seventh-rounder) in exchange for a fourth- and fifth-round pick in the '27 draft.
Recent reports have indicated that the Chiefs were willing to give up a fourth-round pick for Downs well before deadline day, but the Colts held firm until Tuesday, when the Chiefs added the fifth-rounder to seal the deal.
So, how did the Chiefs ultimately fare in the agreement that brought a much-needed pass catcher to Kansas City?
Before any Chiefs fans take offense to "just" a B, hear me out: I think this is a good move that Kansas City had to make. If I were in general manager Brett Veach's shoes as the clock ticked down on deadline day, I would have accepted this same final offer. Still, the Colts got very fair value for their 2023 third-round pick.
A simple trade of Downs for a fourth-rounder would have felt like a better deal for the Chiefs, but I also vastly prefer the way the Chiefs packaged the fourth- and fifth-rounders as opposed to sending a single third-round pick to Indianapolis in the transaction. Meanwhile, the Colts had some leverage because the entire league knew that the Chiefs were in desperate need of a starting-caliber wide receiver.
That point is one of the reasons I struggle to lift the Chiefs' grade above a "B." After an offseason of discussion about how badly Kansas City needed to invest in their wide receiver room, they were left scrambling in November because their current group of pass catchers hasn't been good enough (or healthy enough) to keep the offense afloat.
Tyquan Thornton was looking excellent before his serious ankle injury, and Rashee Rice has been solid when he's been healthy (which may still be a work in progress), but Xavier Worthy hasn't taken a third-year jump, while Jalen Royals and Andrew Armstrong haven't made much of their respective workloads. Rookie Cyrus Allen hasn't had a serious role, despite his training camp hype. This was a predictable problem with the Chiefs' roster well before the season began.
There's one other major unknown in Downs' future that will ultimately determine how this trade is viewed. Right now, Downs is only guaranteed to be in Kansas City through the remainder of this season. He's in the final year of his rookie contract and is scheduled to hit free agency in the spring. That, of course, is part of the reason he was available for roughly a third-round value, while players like Brian Thomas Jr., with additional team control on their current contracts, didn't get moved at the deadline. There was no urgency for many of those other teams and players.
The Colts essentially had to trade Downs on Tuesday, and the Chiefs essentially had to add a receiver. Therefore, the leverage game evened out and both sides got what they wanted.
You'd also be well within your rights to ask me why I care about a fifth-round pick at all. The NFL Draft is always a bit of a guessing game, and Day 3 draftees rarely become impact players. That's all completely fair—it's also one of the reasons I'd be a pick-hoarder as a general manager. Keeping more picks means taking more swings on players who could round out your roster at very low salaries for years to come.
In the 2026 NFL Draft, the Chiefs had two fifth-round picks: running back Emmett Johnson, who has flashed budding-star potential , and the aforementioned Allen, who had plenty of training camp hype but has only five catches so far this season.
In 2025, the Chiefs' fourth- and fifth-rounders were Royals and linebacker Jeffrey Bassa: two players who haven't yet made an impact in the pros.
What about 2024's Jared Wiley, Jaden Hicks, and Hunter Nourzad? Hicks is carrying that group as KC's third safety, while the others are organizational depth. 2023's Chamarri Conner and BJ Thompson? Conner is a valued starter in the final year of his rookie deal, while Thompson never stuck. 2020's L'Jarius Sneed and Mike Danna? Those were massive hits, but they came many, many draft classes ago.
All of that is to reiterate why I'd always like to have a few more draft picks, given the opportunity, but I am certainly not bent out of shape about the extra selection needed to seal the deal to bring Downs to KC.
Much like any overachieving student, perhaps you're not content with a "B" and would like to raise your grade later in the year with some extra credit. The Chiefs can do that, too!
If the Chiefs enjoy their time with Downs throughout the second half of this 2026 season (and if Downs is willing to forego full-on free agency for the sake of pairing up with Patrick Mahomes for the next act of his career), Kansas City could pay Downs and ensure that he won't just be a half-season rental. Even if Downs does leave in free agency, the Chiefs would be able to recoup some value with his addition to the compensatory pick formula, which would soften the blow.
The Chiefs absolutely did not get ripped off. The Colts certainly didn't get swindled. This is about as fair of a mid-level trade as you'll find between a contender and a rebuilder, and both teams are better off now than they were on Tuesday morning.

title: Chiefs Cut Ties With Special Teams Ace, Shuffle Roster and Cap After Josh Downs Trade
full_text:
It's been a busy week for the Kansas City Chiefs as they attempt to move on from a win over the New York Jets and gear up for a road contest versus the Atlanta Falcons. Although the 2026 NFL trade deadline is in the books, general manager Brett Veach's work is far from done.
On Wednesday, Kansas City completed some roster moves and also appears to have made a tweak to the salary cap sheet in response to the club's trade for former Indianapolis Colts receiver Josh Downs.
Let's dive into the latest Chiefs transactions and what they could mean for the rest of the season.
In a Wednesday morning tweet on X, the Chiefs announced that the Downs trade is official. It's him and a 2027 seventh-round pick coming to KC in exchange for fourth- and fifth-round picks in the same NFL Draft.
In order to make room for Downs on the 53-man roster, wide receiver Nikko Remigio was waived. The 2023 undrafted free agent is now available to be claimed by all 31 other NFL teams but could always pursue a return to Kansas City if he clears waivers.
We have traded for WR Josh Downs. We have waived WR Nikko Remigio and DE Jack Pyburn. pic.twitter.com/bdZIgClbIW
Remigio, who turned 27 a week ago, was in his fourth year with the team. The former Fresno State standout has 72 offensive snaps and 202 special teams reps to his name as a Chief, including respective marks of two and 55 in 2026. Remigio played in five regular-season games in 2024 before seeing that total increase to 14 last campaign. He'd appeared in all eight contests to date this season.
Assuming it isn't Remigio being back on the practice squad and elevated for game day, it'll be interesting to see who handles the return duties for the Chiefs. Remigio had 12 kickoff returns and 14 punt returns this year, including a big-time 69-yard return that was wiped by a penalty on Sunday.
Options for the vacant special teams role include rookies Cyrus Allen and Emmett Johnson, as well as running back Brashard Smith once he comes off injured reserve . Downs has 32 punt returns and a pair of kickoff returns on his resume, although his projected role on offense could keep him out of special teams dealings.
The Chiefs have also waived defensive end Jack Pyburn, whom the franchise originally claimed off waivers at the end of August when roster cuts were happening. Like Remigio, he may be a practice squad candidate.
No corresponding addition has been revealed as of the publishing of this article, but reading the tea leaves could hint at defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott officially rejoining the 53-man roster from the physically unable to perform list.
Veach and company found themselves strapped for cash at the deadline, leaving Downs as one of the more affordable and sensible pieces that wouldn't require a ton of cap gymnastics to fit under the league-allotted threshold.
Kansas City wound up pulling the contract lever of linebacker Nick Bolton to make sufficient room for Downs' expiring rookie deal.
Shared by Michael Ginnitti of Spotrac , $6.76M of Bolton's salary was converted into a signing bonus, giving the team another $3.3M in space to work with. The polarizing defensive stopper now carries a 2027 cap hit of $22.6M with $7.6M in dead money if released, further signaling that he's in the club's plans for next season.
The #Chiefs converted $6.76M of LB Nick Bolton's salary into signing bonus, creating $3.3M of 2026 cap space. Updated Cap Hits (dead) 2026: $15.8M ($23.5M) 2027: $22.6M ($7.6M)
If the Chiefs wanted to lower that number to below $20M, they could always sign Bolton to an offseason contract extension. Considering that he's still only 26 years old, that outlook seems to be favorable.

title: The 5 Most Disappointing Chargers Players So Far This Season
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have had a rough season to say the least.
There are always certain expectations for every player going into any season. Some perform better than predicted, however, that is simply not the case for every single athlete that steps foot on the gridiron.
Here are five guys who have not moved the needle in a positive direction when it comes to overall execution.
Justin Herbert has arguably been the biggest disappointment of the 2026 season.
Entering the year, he was expected to be the centerpiece of an offense capable of competing with the best teams in the NFL. Instead, his performances have become a major part of the team’s struggles. Herbert has thrown for 1,591 yards, six touchdowns and 11 interceptions. His 70.4 passer rating is a troubling number for a quarterback with his experience and ability. Even more concerning, he has been sacked 31 times.
The turnovers have been particularly damaging. Herbert has struggled to consistently protect the football, putting additional pressure on an offense that already has difficulty sustaining drives. Herbert always seems to be on the short end of the stick, so that surely doesn't help. However the elite quarterback needs to put up better performances regardless.
Omarion Hampton entered the season with an opportunity to establish himself as one of the most important pieces of the offensive attack. Unfortunately, his production has been inconsistent and the running game has not developed into the reliable weapon the team desperately needs.
The lack of carries have definitely been a factor, but still you would like to see a little more outta him.
There is still plenty of potential, but his first eight games have not delivered the kind of impact expected from such an important young offensive player.
Cole Strange has become another concerning part of an offensive line that has struggled to provide consistent protection. His individual performance has been especially disappointing considering how important interior blocking is to the success of the entire offense.
The veteran guard has struggled to consistently win his assignments, creating problems for both the passing and running games. When interior protection breaks down, quarterbacks have less time to make decisions, while running backs have fewer opportunities to find open lanes.
He has not provided the level of stability expected from an experienced offensive lineman.
This might not shock some people, but Quentin Johnston has not shown enough this season. The whole offense is a disaster, and he unfortunately is a part of that.
The former TCU standout has had a rough couple years, to say the least. He has improved every year, but cannot put together an elite season.
A first-round pick should provide an exceptional amount of help when they need it the most. The reason they are drafted is to provide what the team has been missing for years. Yet Johnstoin just hasn’t been the player most thought he would be by now. He is a very talented player, but this year hasn't shown much of that.
Donte Jackson rounds out this list after struggling to provide the dependable coverage performances expected from an experienced NFL cornerback.
The secondary has had difficulty consistently limiting opposing passing attacks, and Jackson has experienced some particularly difficult moments during the season.
His performance against the Texans was especially concerning. In the 44-22 defeat, Jackson received a reported overall performance grade of 28.6, highlighting the problems he experienced during one of the team’s worst defensive outings.
Cornerbacks are regularly placed in difficult situations, but experienced players must find ways to limit mistakes and prevent opposing receivers from consistently winning their matchups. Jackson’s struggles have become another example of how problems across the roster have contributed to the team’s disappointing start. He still has the experience to improve, but the secondary needs much more consistency from him moving forward.

title: Chargers Seem More Worried About PR Than Trades, Wins Right Now
full_text:
While trying to send the proper messages to drive narratives, the Los Angeles Chargers are managing to send all the wrong messages.
The fact “messaging” was a theme at all coming from the team and reporters ahead of the NFL trade deadline was pretty telling. Word was, they wanted to hang onto players like Khalil Mack because they didn’t want to send the wrong “message” to the locker room or fans.
But the Chargers then turned around and sent a weird “message” anyway, trading a younger, popular player like Daiyan Henley…to the AFC West rival Denver Broncos.
Weird, and yet it got stranger: The trade fell apart and the latest “message” from the Chargers is just more odd PR work from an 0-8 club.
According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter , the Henley trade fell apart due to confidence the Broncos had with his knee after a physical. The two sides discussed different trade packages to make it work, it seems, then called the whole thing off.
Schefter’s colleague, Ian Rapoport , added this borderline ridiculousness: “Part of the reason was because the Chargers never really wanted to trade Daiyan Henley. They got an offer from the Broncos they couldn’t refuse, so they took it."
Hear that, folks? The Chargers didn’t actually want to trade the player they traded, but only after the trade fell through and the player came back.
By the way, the can’t-miss trade compensation was… a fourth-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
Look, this little nugget from Rapoport was probably the Chargers trying to be nice about this, or even Henley’s agent trying to smooth things over as he goes from a 7-2 locker room back to an 0-8 one. The team that traded him away didn’t want him and it’s pretty clear contract negotiation talks hadn’t worked out, so he’ll be a free agent soon anyway.
But this is just one of those little things to throw on the Chargers pile, which happens to be on fire right now. The Chargers seem misguided, more laser-focused on PR and messaging than anything else.
Obviously, that’s not 100 percent the case. But it all adds up to a team that feels unfocused and doesn’t know what direction it wants to really go in, which is summed up pretty well by the winless record and move-less trade deadline.

title: The Chargers Have a Legit Chance of Landing Newly Released Wide Receiver
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers should take a serious look at Hollywood Brown. The Sooners alumni recently got released by the Philadelphia Eagles and now is l ooking for another team.
Brown has built his game around acceleration, movement and turning a small opening into a big play. Those qualities are valuable for a team looking to make its passing attack more dangerous.
For the Chargers, the appeal would be about more than adding another name to the receiver room. A player who threatens defenses vertically may create easier opportunities underneath for the rest of the offense. Also, looking towards the future is honestly the best thing now.
There would still be questions before making a move.
Brown’s role, health, contract expectations and the team’s cap space would matter. The Chargers would need to decide whether his skill set matches the coaching staff’s plans and whether the price makes sense. Speed is exciting, but a roster decision has to work beyond the highlight plays.
The connection between the franchise and Brown runs deeper than people think. Joe Hortiz was the director of college scouting for the Ravens for many years. He eventually became director of player personnel, which led him to having a big role in drafting Brown.
Having connections like this really makes a difference. Every year we see players head to organizations where they had previous relationships with either the staff or fellow athletes.
Brown is most dangerous when timing and trust are clear. The offense would need to get him involved early, rather than asking him to wait for a few deep chances each game. Screens, motion, crossing routes and vertical patterns could help make his presence felt. A varied role would make it harder for opponents to predict where the ball is going.
There is no guarantee the Chargers will pursue Brown, and a potential fit should not be confused with a completed deal. Still, the idea is easy to understand. The Bolts could consider a receiver whose speed might change the geometry of the field and give its offense another dimension. If the opportunity is realistic and the terms are right, Brown could be an intriguing addition. The Chargers would not need him to carry the passing game alone. They would need him to win matchups, create space and make defenses pay when they leave him room. In a league where one explosive play can swing a game, that kind of weapon is worth evaluating.
It was clear that the Eagles signing Hollywood Brown was never going to work from the start of the regular season when he was a healthy scratch. title: What Has Been Joe Hortiz's Biggest Mistake in 2026?
full_text:
Every general manager makes decisions that look better on paper than they do once the season gets underway.
Some make encouraging moves, important decisions, and reasons to believe the organization is heading in the right direction. For Joe Hortiz of the Los Angeles Chargers , those factors have not been met to the full extent.
When evaluating Hortiz’s work this year, one particular area stands out. It isn’t necessarily the flashiest position on the roster , nor is it a decision that will dominate every conversation among fans. But it could have a much bigger impact on the team’s ceiling than people realize.
The biggest mistake Hortiz made in 2026 was not doing enough to strengthen the offensive line around Justin Herbert.
This isn’t a new conversation. Protecting Herbert has been a recurring challenge, and the organization has spent considerable time trying to establish consistency up front. For a quarterback with his arm talent, mobility, and ability to make plays outside the structure of an offense, there is little reason to leave him constantly dealing with unnecessary pressure.
Hortiz had an opportunity to give the offense another layer of security. Adding an experienced offensive lineman could have provided valuable depth and prevented the team from having to rely so heavily on its existing options. Instead, the position remained an area that deserved more attention. And when you’re building around a quarterback like Herbert, this is not somewhere you want to take unnecessary chances. I could give you all the statistics in the world backing up these claims, but the majority of people have a good idea what those numbers would look like.
There is also a bigger picture worth considering . The offense has already experienced enough changes over the past several seasons. Different coordinators, different systems, and adjustments to personnel have all played a role in shaping the unit. Establishing stability up front should be one of the organization’s main priorities. Hortiz deserves credit for recognizing the importance of surrounding Herbert with talent, but that responsibility extends beyond adding weapons and making headline grabbing acquisitions. Sometimes the most important addition is the player who keeps a defensive lineman from getting anywhere near your quarterback.
That is particularly important when your franchise quarterback is the centerpiece of everything you’re trying to accomplish. Hortiz has shown that he understands what this organization needs to become a legitimate contender. But if there is one area where his approach deserved more attention this offseason, it’s protecting the player who gives this team its best chance to win.
A roster can have plenty of talent, but none of it matters if the quarterback doesn’t have enough time to use it.
